title: Ogun community seeks support on tourism
content:
Traditional leaders of Ebute-Igbooro in Yewa North Local Government Area of Ogun State have called on the state government to provide infrastructure and other facilities to transform Oleyo Waterfall into a major cultural and tourist attraction.
They said the ancient waterfall had existed for generations and historically played an important role in the cultural and spiritual life of the people.
The Elebute of Ebute-Igbooro, Alhaji Amusa Dosumu, in statement made available to our correspondent on Saturday, said the waterfall was situated on Ebute-Igbooro land and belonged to the community.
Oba Dosumu spoke about the cultural significance of the Oleyo Waterfall, saying the community had continued to associate the spring with positive experiences and good water.
“There are many benefits because this Oleyo water does not tolerate evil. We see that it brings good water,” he said.
The traditional ruler appealed to the Ogun State Government to support the community in developing and promoting the site, particularly as part of efforts to preserve Yoruba cultural heritage and attract visitors.
Similarly, the Balogun of Ebute-Igbooro, Jeremiah Ijiola, described Oleyo as a remarkable natural and cultural heritage whose potential, he said, had not been fully explored.
Ijiola said members of the community had traditionally visited the location to pray, adding that the spring had been associated with local traditional practices for generations.
“Nobody ever thought that something as wonderful and awe-inspiring as this existed here,” he said.
He explained that prayers and traditional activities had historically been conducted at the location, adding that the community had stories of rainfall occurring during such occasions.
Ijiola urged the government to take ownership of the development process by providing infrastructure and facilities that could make Oleyo Waterfall accessible to tourists and visitors.
He drew a comparison with the development of Olumo Rock in Abeokuta, saying Oleyo Waterfall could similarly be transformed into a destination capable of attracting visitors from within and outside the country.
“Just like they took care of Olumo, how they renovated Olumo Rock so that it became a tourist centre—where people come from far away distances,” he said.
The Youth Leader of Ebute-Igbooro, Emmanuel Akan, also said the waterfall was not a recent discovery, explaining that the existence and traditional significance of the spring had been passed down through generations.
“Oleyo has been here long before we were born. Long before our fathers gave birth to us, we heard that Oleyo was here and that they used to worship it. So, it is not a recent discovery,” Akan said.
He reiterated the community’s claim that the surrounding area belonged to Ebute-Igbooro, adding that the spring had historically been used by their forefathers.
“The fathers before us who gave birth to my own parents were already worshipping it here in Ebute,” he said.
Akan also spoke about the growing interest in the water, claiming that visitors from different parts of Nigeria and abroad had been coming to the location to collect it for prayers and traditional purposes.
“As it is right now, people come all the way from abroad, from Abuja, and from everywhere to fetch this water,” he said.
He appealed to the Ogun State Government to intervene by providing infrastructure and helping the community transform the location into a modern cultural and tourism destination.
“We want the government to assist us with it—to help elevate our Yoruba cultural heritage, to modernise it, and to turn it into something great and remarkable,” Akan said.
He specifically called for improved access roads, fencing, renovation and other basic facilities that could make the site suitable for visitors.

title: ‘Always kind, never argued’: Colleagues on Manipur musician killed in Delhi
content:
Chongtham Vikram Singh grew up in a family steeped in music. His mother Chongtham Kamala, now 85, is one of the defining voices of Manipuri music and cinema. She sang in Matamgi Manipur (1972) — the first Manipuri feature film in which her melodious voice earned her the moniker ‘Lata Mangeshkar of Manipur’.
But Singh set out to build a musical identity of his own and chose the electric guitar to find himself. He went on to become a pioneering guitarist of Manipur’s early rock scene.
Beaten to death in Delhi’s Kilokari village after objecting to a group making noise outside his residence on Monday, the 54-year-old leaves behind a significant musical career that ranged from Manipur’s early Western music scene to years spent teaching and mentoring young musicians in the Capital.
Those who have worked with him – from guitarist Sachidananda Angom to folk musician Mame Khan of Coke Studio India fame – remember him as someone who was “always kind, helpful” and who “never had arguments with anyone.”
Singh is survived by his wife, Joshna, 54, and their son Yaiphaba. The 20-year-old is a law student.
On Tuesday, fellow musicians, family members and well-wishers held a candlelight vigil at the historic Kangla fort in Imphal, demanding justice.
Manipur Chief Minister Yumnam Khemchand Singh, in a letter to his Delhi counterpart Rekha Gupta, requested that a fair probe be conducted under the direct supervision of senior police leadership. The Manipur CM also asked for reinforced security measures across Delhi localities with significant populations of students and working professionals from Manipur and other northeastern states.
Story continues below this ad
Originally from Lourung Purel Leikai in Imphal West district, Singh was the eldest son of Kamla and Chongtham Birendra, a medical doctor. A calm Kamla, sitting quietly at the family home, told The Indian Express, “Vikram (Singh) and his brother Vivek always loved to perform as kids. They always participated in school entertainment events.”
Even as he forged a separate path for himself, Singh, for years, accompanied his mother to the radio station – she had gained immense popularity as a broadcast singer at All India Radio (AIR), Imphal – regularly for recordings. The experience left a lasting impression on him. Singh auditioned, too, and was also approved as a child artist at AIR. He would play the accordion then.
“Since his mother was associated with AIR Imphal, he got to meet some of the most significant artistes in Manipur and learned under the tutelage of renowned names,” says Angom, former lead guitarist of well-known band Imphal Talkies and The Howlers.
Singh began as the lead guitarist of famous Manipur band Ultra Vires formed in the late ’80s. He had just finished his class X then. This was a time when rock music was at its peak in the state and Singh immersed himself in the sound. To hone his skills further, he later enrolled at Trinity School of Music in Kolkata, where he studied classical guitar.
Story continues below this ad
He then went on to play with Phoenix (later Phynyx) and then Eastern Dark, remembered for its socially conscious themes. Singh is remembered by his friends and colleagues for his fine, highly skilled guitar playing. Almost two decades ago, Singh moved to Delhi and began giving lessons in electric guitar. This is when Angom became his student.
‘He could really light up a room’
“He would also come down to the studio for the recording of various Imphal Talkies albums. We would often do these informal jam sessions. He was a really good guitarist and, as a person, one of the nicest guys you would ever meet. He was always kind, helpful and could really light up a room. It (his death) is a terrible loss,” said Angom.
When Singh came to Delhi, he began by teaching at Arttree Academy of Music & Performing Arts in Kamla Nagar. Classical guitar instructor Tej Gurung, who teaches at Delhi School of Music, met Singh at Arttree, where the two became colleagues and friends. “He taught electric guitar; I taught classical guitar. He was a wonderful person, the sweetest guy and also a brilliant guitar player. He’s got to be super famous in Manipur because he was very good,” says Gurung.
After a while, Gurung introduced him to Hitesh Madaan, the guitarist for Euphoria — the popular folk rock band formed by Palash Sen in 1988. Soon, Singh began teaching at Madan’s ARIA music school in Rajouri Garden. What was unique about Singh was that teaching, like it is for many musicians, was not a part-time job for him; he really enjoyed helping younger musicians find their own way around the guitar. He also mentored students at home.
Story continues below this ad
Alongside his teaching career, Singh continued playing with various musicians, including Delhi-based classic rock and jazz band Fubar Ghetto. For about three years, he worked as a lead guitarist for Khan, who sang in Zoya Akhtar’s Luck By Chance (2009) and does regular international tours.
“It was very heartbreaking to hear about the passing of Vikram – a really kind and lovely person. Playback singer Chinmayi (Sripada) recommended him to me and he played with me until 2016. I also featured him in two of my videos. We did numerous shows together. A hugely talented person and the favourite artiste of my band, he never had arguments with anyone and was always good to others, besides being a musically brilliant artiste. I don’t understand how some people could behave this way with him. It is just really sad,” Khan told The Indian Express.

title: Family of murdered teen pleads for action to solve 36-year cold case
content:
Colleen Walker-Craig's family demands action in Bowraville cold case
In short:
The families of Colleen Walker-Craig, Evelyn Greenup and Clinton Speedy-Duroux are calling for more action from police to find their children's killer.
Homicide detectives are in northern NSW engaging with locals in Macksville, who they hope may have information regarding Ms Walker-Craig's remains.
What's next?
Police say they have not previously targeted the Macksville community, north of Bowraville, and anyone with information is urged to come forward.
WARNING: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander readers are advised this article contains the names and images of people who have died.
After grieving for more than three decades, an Indigenous family is demanding police "stop appealing and just go out" as homicide detectives return to northern NSW in a bid to find the body of murdered teenager Colleen Walker-Craig.
The 16-year-old was last seen at Bowraville, north of Coffs Harbour, on September 13, 1990.
Her mother, Muriel Craig, has renewed her pleas for police to solve the 36-year-old cold case.
"I know that there's people who live in the Bowraville community who know what happened to Colleen," she said.
"Sometimes I think the police don't believe me.
"I know they haven't questioned these people. I can't wait any longer."
The teenager’s weighted-down clothes were discovered in the Nambucca River months after her disappearance, but her body has never been found.
In an inquest, a state coroner declared her dead and most likely murdered.
A $1 million reward has been offered for information leading to the recovery of her remains.
Today, detectives arrived in Macksville, just south-east of Bowraville, for a week of community engagement, appealing for new information.
Four-year-old Evelyn Greenup and 16-year-old Clinton Speedy-Duroux, who were also First Nations children, disappeared in the area about the same time.
Their remains were discovered in 1991, but no-one has ever been convicted of their murders.
Separate $1 million rewards have also been offered for information that leads to police solving their cases as well.
Asking for answers
Detective Superintendent Joe Doueihi did not directly respond when asked about the family's concerns but said this week's community engagement could help the investigation.
He said officers would be stationed at Macksville's Phillip Hughes Pavillion to speak with locals until Friday afternoon, after a similar operation in Bowraville in 2024.
"It's not just an exercise to keep people happy," Detective Superintendent Doueihi said.
"In 2024, a lot of valuable information was obtained through that.
"What we learned is that we didn't target that community here and we've taken those lessons on board."
Detective Superintendent Doueihi said loyalties could change over the course of 36 years.
"We believe that people in this community didn't present in 2024, and we're giving them that opportunity now," he said.
Colleen Walker-Craig's brother Lucas Craig urged those with information to contact police.
"Think about the families, how long we've been suffering with this," he said.
"This was three quarters of my life that I've had to deal with this.
"Going to work and coming home to your family and seeing your parents upset every day because there's nothing they can do."
Mr Craig said the family's relationship with police was "not as strong as we'd like it to be".
Elijah Duroux, the nephew of Clinton Speedy-Duroux, said his family felt like the investigation had stagnated.
He said they were not informed police would be in Macksville until this morning and were not informed when police divers led new searches of the Nambucca River late last year.
"Don't you think my grandfather and grandmother deserve to know when there's stuff going on in regards to their son's murder?" Mr Duroux said.
Evelyn Greenup's mother, Rebecca Stadhams, released a statement through NSW Police, calling on people to come forward.
"Maybe you have carried this information for years. Maybe you were afraid to speak. Maybe you think what you know is too small or doesn't matter," she said.
"But it might matter. It might be the piece of information that finally helps us find the truth about what happened to Evelyn.
"After all these years, I am asking you to think about my little girl."

title: 19 Years of the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples
content: 19 Years of the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Country Global agnes Sun, 09/13/2026 - 13:49 Issues Human Rights Program 5 Main Image September 13, 2026, marks 19 years since the United Nations General Assembly adopted the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (UNDRIP). In a historic vote on September 13, 2007, 144 countries voted for the Declaration, 11 abstained, and only four (Australia, Canada, New Zealand, and the United States) voted against it. Since 2007, all four countries, including the United States, have reversed their positions and now officially endorse the Declaration. The Declaration is the outcome of 25 years of hard negotiations. The rights spelled out in the document "constitute the minimum standards for the survival, dignity, and well-being of the Indigenous Peoples of the world." The Declaration protects the collective rights and individual rights of Indigenous Peoples in relation to self-government, land, education, employment, health, and other areas. The Declaration also requires countries to consult with Indigenous Peoples with the goal of obtaining their consent on matters that concern them. As explained by former UN Special Rapporteur on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, James Anaya (Apache and Purépecha), the right of self-determination is "to be full and equal participants in the creation of the institutions of government under which they live and, further, to live within a governing institutional order in which they are perpetually in control of their own destinies." While several countries have made steps towards aligning their policies with the standards enshrined in the Declaration, an implementation gap remains. "Governments around the world must honor their responsibilities to move from Declaration endorsement to adoption and align their domestic laws and policies with the rights, self-governance, and self-determination of Indigenous Peoples," says Cultural Survival Executive Director Aimee Roberson (Choctaw and Chickasaw). Cultural Survival has put together this interactive timeline to display the history of the Declaration and progress towards its implementation since 2007. title: Lost oyster beds rediscovered thanks to Gaelic and Scots language
content:
Lost oyster beds rediscovered thanks to Gaelic and Scots language
- Published
Long lost oyster beds on the West Coast of Scotland have been rediscovered thanks to Gaelic and Scots language.
Scientists searched for the inclusion of the Gaelic words for oyster or oysters – eisir, eisirein and eisirean – and oyster habitats like sandy banks or tidal causeways in place names around Scotland's coast.
They then found an oyster bed that had not been previously documented, as well as confirming oysters could have been present at other sites on Mull and Islay.
Native oysters were once abundant in coastal European waters, including Scotland, but now only remnant populations are known to remain due to overharvesting and disease.
Ecology and wildlife experts hope to use the discoveries to help rebuild oyster populations in suitable coastal locations.
The recent findings marked the culmination of several years worth of hard work, titled Project Eisirean.
It is a collaboration between ecology and environment researchers, Gaelic and education experts at the University of Glasgow and local community organisations on the west coast of Scotland.
Dr Anna McGregor, an expert in coastal ecology and a lecturer at the University of Glasgow , had the original idea of locating oysters through traditional place-names, then applying scientific techniques to confirm oyster presence within them.
She explained: "This is a really exciting outcome, for a project that started off looking for the historic distribution of oysters along the West Coast.
"We thought that as native oysters are now really rare throughout Europe, is there a way to look where they used to be, using people's memory and understanding - that can come through place names.
"We found two areas with oyster in the name, both on Mull, and after about two years we found another one on Lewis. Then we broadened the search to look for habitat related names, like sand banks."
The group then examined those locations for factors like the sea bed and the level of the water flow.
Dr McGregor hopes the team can build on their findings through continued work with local communities in Islay and Mull, alongside oyster bed restoration and protection work in key areas.
The research team will now trial the feasibility of a mobile oyster hatchery, in the hope it could both supply oyster larvae to coastal communities and help rebuild oyster beds in various areas.
The first mobile hatchery is being trialled in Millport, with plans to trial more in the future.
Dr McGregor said: "What we are hopping is to connect knowledge of the past, where shellfish was an important part of people's diets, to future improvement.
"We want to look where shellfish used to be, where communities had a connection with them, and develop that again.
"A small scale hatchery like this [on Millport] can be sustainable on an island, and really help people to connect with them.
"Seeing oysters life cycle can help people understand why it's important to keep them in the wild, and then get the numbers back up to levels where we can harvest them for lots of purposes."
The Native Oyster Restoration Alliance – NORA – coordinates projects across Europe to enhance the restoration of flat oyster reefs.
Hein Sas, the secretary of NORA, said: "The Eisirean project can serve as an example for other projects on how cultural heritage can help to identify suitable restoration sites."

title: Aboriginal man's fight for justice after alleged historical abuse at hospital
content:
Uncle Benjamin 'BJ' Cruse's fight for justice after alleged historical healthcare abuse
Uncle Benjamin 'BJ' Cruse says he has lived with a lifetime of trauma stemming from a few days in hospital.
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander readers are advised that this article contains the names and images of an Indigenous person who has died, used with the permission of family.
Warning: This story contains details that may be distressing for some readers.
As a young boy, he was treated for dysentery, an intestinal infection which causes severe diarrhoea, with his siblings at Macleay District Hospital on the New South Wales Mid North Coast.
The Yuin and Monaroo elder remembers being placed on a verandah with his brother and sister at the health facility now known as Kempsey District Hospital, and the rooms being partitioned with "hessian bag material".
"That's where Aboriginal people were kept," he said.
It was here Mr Cruse alleges he was physically and emotionally abused, including being slapped multiple times on the face by a nurse.
He said he was told to kneel on the bed with his back straight, as books were stacked on his head.
"When the nurse heard the books fall on the floor … she yanked me off the bed and slapped me on both sides of the face,"he said.
The now 72-year-old also claimed being given apron strings to hold in each hand and forced to follow the nurse around the ward as she treated other patients.
"If she walked too fast, I'd pull both apron strings undone and she'd turn around and slap me on both sides of the face," he said.
The almost-week long ordeal left Mr Cruse with psychological issues, he said.
His sister, Aunty Rhonda Cruse-Rawiri, recalled being kept in a dark, separate room away from other patients.
"I could see out of that room where they had all the non-Aboriginal kids and it was really bright in there, all the toys and a big rocking horse," she said.
"I remember standing at the door waiting to go out and the nurse came … shooing us back in the room.
"And the [hospital] gown we had [on] had A-B-O across the back."
Their father, Uncle Ossie Cruse, who is now in his early 90s, also remembered the gowns from when he picked his children up from the hospital.
"And I thought, 'Wow, we're out of here'," he told Australian Story in 2017.
"I just grabbed the kids, and we never even went to see the people. We just took them out and went home."
'An insult'
Now, Mr Cruse is calling for an apology and "proper and just" compensation for his alleged abuse, taking his demands to the state government, as well as the United Nations Permanent Forum on Indigenous Issues.
But he said on multiple occasions the government referred him to existing schemes, including the NSW Stolen Generations Reparation Scheme, and the National Redress Scheme created following the Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse schemes, both of which he is not eligible for.
"This is something that has gone under the radar, it's fallen through the cracks and just because it [the alleged abuse] doesn't meet that criteria," Mr Cruse said.
"I believe it shouldn't give the government the option to opt out of their responsibility."
However, since engaging lawyers, Mr Cruse said the local health district had now offered him compensation.
Though for him, he said it was not enough to make it right.
"I would receive a payment of $30,000 in the hand and to me that is an insult," he said.
"The government is holding me at ransom … knowing I can't fight the matter in court and that's why I wanted to bring the matter to the nation."
A Mid North Coast Local Health District spokesperson said in a statement it "does not comment on matters that are the subject of legal proceedings".
"The NSW government acknowledges and remembers the survivors of historical abuse and the past failures of governments and institutions to protect them," they said.
"The NSW government remains committed to ensuring survivors of historical abuse receive appropriate support and justice."
It also said all government agencies dealing with civil claims of child abuse followed guiding principles to make "litigation a less traumatic experience for victims".
'Deemed the right thing to do'
Mr Cruse said he and his siblings were taken to the Macleay District Hospital when he was about five years old, making it the late 1950s or early 1960s.
According to the Macleay River Historical Society, segregation ended at the hospital in July 1964.
Former nurse, scholar and labour historian, Odette Best, said this was "a very thick and murky era" for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander staff and patients.
"It was deemed the right thing to do that Indigenous people were not allowed to be nursed in the same ward as non-Indigenous people," Dr Best, a Gorreng Gorreng, Boonthamurra and Yugambeh woman said.
"The contested care that has actually been inflicted upon Aboriginal people has been full of abuse and neglect … [and] has left very deep ongoing scars for many, many Indigenous people."
Dr Best acknowledged while many nurses "do absolutely amazing work and do care for our communities", there were historical aspects that needed to be reconciled.
"Nursing has really got this huge history of this contested care that has really never been spoken about, talked about or addressed as a profession … that we actually participated in some pretty horrendous acts against Indigenous people,"she said.
National Justice Project CEO George Newhouse said there were still remnants of past policies within the healthcare system.
"People can die as a result of a doctor, or a nurse, or a clinician having a closed mind," he said.
"So even today we see hangovers of the segregation in the past and the low standard of healthcare provided to First Nations people."
Fear of being taken
As a child, Mr Cruse and his family moved around as his father Uncle Ossie Cruse followed the fruit and vegetable picking seasons as a seasonal worker, which led them to stay near Kempsey.
"For those 11 years up until 1967, we lived in tents, on the riverbanks, or on the beaches … and dad fished off the beach with nets or worked in the timber industry as a sleeper cutter," Mr Cruse said.
"So, we were what they called itinerant workers, living on the fringe camps."
The family eventually moved to Sydney where Mr Cruse and Ms Cruse-Rawiri remembered the NSW Aborigines Welfare Board visited their home.
Up until the late 1960s, the welfare board previously named the Aborigines Protection Board, controlled the lives and affairs of Aboriginal people in NSW by enforcing policies of segregation, assimilation, child removal and wage withholding.
"They went through the house, checked all our sheets, checked the cupboards, checked everything," Ms Cruse-Rawiri said.
"When my dad came home that afternoon he [went] into the room, and we had these little brown suitcases, and dad came back out to us and said whatever you can fit into those little bags you put it in cause we are leaving.
"My nan used to say if you see a car coming … you run as fast as you can and you hide.
"We were never stolen, but we grew up with the fear of being taken."
Ever since, Mr Cruse has been an advocate for his community and was involved in the land rights movement for decades.
His latest fight is his most personal: he is hoping to continue advocating for those who may have fallen through the cracks, like him.
"It's something that needs to be picked up and addressed because [there's been] much suffering for [our] people and their descendants … and it's still outstanding today," he said.
"I believe this will go a long way to healing."

title: Braziliaanse inheemse leider Raoni (94) heeft kanker en krijgt palliatieve zorg
content:
Raoni, de bekende Braziliaanse inheemse leider, heeft kanker en krijgt palliatieve zorg. Dat heeft zijn organisatie, het Instituto Raoni, bekendgemaakt. Raoni (94) reisde jarenlang de wereld rond om de zaak van de inheemse volkeren en het Amazonegebied onder de aandacht te brengen.
Braziliaanse inheemse leider Raoni (94) heeft kanker en krijgt palliatieve zorg
Recent kreeg Raoni de diagnose van een agressieve kanker aan het spijsverteringsstelsel, zegt het Instituto Raoni op sociale media. De inheemse leider kampt al langer met gezondheidsproblemen.
In juni werd hij in de stad São Paulo in het ziekenhuis opgenomen vanwege een ernstige darmobstructie die door een tumor was veroorzaakt. Hij werd geopereerd en keerde terug naar de stad Peixoto de Azevedo, in de Braziliaanse staat Mato Grosso. Die stad ligt dicht bij het Amazonegebied waar Raoni is opgegroeid.
Daar krijgt hij nu palliatieve zorg. "Gezien zijn leeftijd, zijn klinische toestand en de hoge risico's van agressieve behandelingen hebben de artsen hiervoor gekozen", zegt het Instituto Raoni. Hij wordt thuis verzorgd, "omringd door zijn familie, gemeenschap en gespecialiseerde zorgteams".
De zorg omvat ook interculturele en spirituele ondersteuning waarmee zijn inheemse afkomst wordt geëerd en traditionele genezers naast medisch personeel worden ingezet.
"Op dit moment is onze prioriteit ervoor te zorgen dat leider Raoni goed verzorgd wordt, zich comfortabel voelt en dicht bij zijn familie en zijn volk is", luidt het nog.
"We willen deze informatie transparant delen, maar vragen ook om respect voor zijn privacy, zijn behoefte aan rust en de beslissingen van zijn familie.
Raoni is een van de meest vooraanstaande voorvechters van de bescherming van de rechten van inheemse volkeren en van het Amazonewoud.
Al sinds de jaren 70 reisde hij de wereld rond om het bewustzijn te vergroten. In de jaren 80 verscheen hij aan de zijde van presidenten, pausen en artiesten om aandacht te vragen voor de bescherming van het Amazonewoud.
Raoni had als lid van het Kayapo-volk een lipschotel, wat aangeeft dat een krijger bereid is om voor zijn land te sterven.

title: [Research] The Energy–Water–Food Nexus Under Abundant Clean Power
source: OpenAlex (Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research))
content:
The Energy–Water–Food Nexus Under Abundant Clean Power
Authors/Creators
Description
Abundant clean electricity—delivered in the 1–3¢/kWh band now emerging in the world’s best solar and wind geographies—fundamentally rewrites the economics of water and food security. As the report states, “lifting, moving, purifying, growing, and cooling all require energy,” and historically that energy has been expensive, unreliable, and fossil‑based. Under cheap renewables, the binding constraint across the energy‑water‑food nexus dissolves, enabling a structural shift rather than an incremental improvement.
Seawater reverse osmosis operating near 2.2 kWh/m³ and powered by two‑cent electricity delivers water at ~$0.45/m³, pushing desalination from luxury to baseline infrastructure for coastal cities and agricultural zones. Vertical farming—long constrained by lighting and HVAC costs—sees unit economics fall 37%, from $6.85/kg to $4.30/kg, enabling controlled‑environment agriculture to move from niche greens to staple vegetables and fruiting crops. Green ammonia reaches cost parity with fossil ammonia at ~2.5¢/kWh, unlocking decarbonized fertilizer, long‑duration energy storage, and clean marine fuel from the same electrolyzer base. Solar‑powered cold chains close the gap between 65% coverage in high‑income countries and 4–15% in LMICs, cutting post‑harvest losses that reach 37% in Sub‑Saharan Africa.
The report formalizes these interactions through the Compound Nexus Multiplier, showing that simultaneous relief across energy, water, and food domains produces welfare gains far larger than siloed interventions. It introduces the GRID Framework—Generate, Reclaim, Intensify, Distribute—as a coupled portfolio that must be built in parallel to capture compounding benefits. As the document emphasizes, “sequencing them serially forfeits the compound gains that make the transition worth its capital cost.” The conclusion is clear: abundant clean power is not merely cheaper electricity—it is a new substrate on which climate‑resilient development can be built.

title: When Pammal Sambanda Mudaliar took Tamil theatre to Ceylon
content:
Pammal Sambanda Mudaliar’s magnum opus Nataka Medai Ninaivugal is a fascinating study of Tamil theatre of the late 19th and early 20th centuries, as seen through the journey of the Suguna Vilasa Sabha. Written in excruciating detail in most parts, this work documents the important role played by the Sabha in creating a renaissance in theatre, nurturing several talents and troupes. Ahead of Sambanda Mudaliar’s 62nd death anniversary on September 24, a look at the Suguna Vilasa Sabha’s performances in Ceylon and how they inspired the formation of a theatre group in the island nation.
In 1909, Sambanda Mudaliar and a few friends went on a private tour to Ceylon and happened to visit the Public Hall in Colombo. They made enquiries about staging performances there and the costs involved. In 1911, the Suguna Vilasa Sabha decided to venture into something it had not attempted before — taking their plays to Ceylon. Sambanda Mudaliar had to deal with multiple challenges in the preparations. One of them stemmed from within the Sabha itself, as a group of Telugu-speaking members protested against the inclusion of a junior artiste, who had just joined, at the expense of seniors. Another challenge was obtaining leave from work for artistes going on the tour, with Sambanda Mudaliar himself intervening on behalf of a few of them to resolve the matter. Costs, too, posed a challenge. This was, however, taken care of, since a drama contractor agreed to take responsibility of the entire production, paying the Sabha a lump sum of Rs 2,500 towards the staging of five plays.
Finally, a nearly 50-member delegation travelled to Colombo, where it was welcomed by a group of prominent Tamils led by the eminent lawyer Sir A. Kanagasabai. Sambanda Mudaliar later wrote in his book Naan Kanda Naadaga Kalaignargal that the tour drew large crowds and began with the staging of Leelavathi Sulochana. Among the audience for the play was Warwick Major, who held a long lease on the Public Hall and regularly let it out for performances. This man would later etch himself in the history of Madras for giving it its first permanent cinema house, the Electric Theatre on Mount Road. Today, this building houses the Philatelic Bureau. The other plays staged included Manohara, Galava Charithram, Amaladityan and Sarangadhara. The Governor of Ceylon Sir Henry Edward McCallum, presided over the performance of Amaladityan (an adaptation of Hamlet). Such was the success of the plays that Sir Kanagasabai requested Sambanda Mudaliar to stage another play in aid of the Governor’s Tuberculosis Fund. The Sabha staged the comedy Kaadhalar Kangal and donated half the proceeds, net of expenses, to the fund.
Sambanda Mudaliar writes of the warm hospitality accorded to the Suguna Vilasa Sabha members by people from across all sections of the society.
The Sabha embarked on its second visit to Ceylon in May 1913, this time including Jaffna in their itinerary. After staging five plays at Colombo, the troupe travelled to Jaffna, where things ran into rough weather. Sambanda Mudaliar took ill (which he attributes to a severe bout of indigestion brought on by his inability to refuse the grand hospitality at various gatherings in Colombo!), and adding to the troupe’s discomfort were the less-than-satisfactory arrangements made by the contractor for the performing venue as well as their stay. It was decided by the Suguna Vilasa Sabha committee to refund the advance taken and cancel the tour.
The development led to rumours that the tour was being cancelled because the Sabha was dissatisfied with the reception it had received. The people of Jaffna took it to be an affront to their reputation as gracious hosts. Fortunately, the District Judge, MS Pinto happened to be Sambanda Mudaliar’s classmate at Madras Presidency College. At his behest took a group of lawyers took it upon themselves to ensure that the members were provided with better accommodation and facilities. The tour eventually continued and earned the sabha a surplus of Rs. 1,500, which went towards its building fund. As on its earlier visit, a benefit performance was staged at the request of a few prominent personalities, this time in aid of the Jaffna University.
During its silver jubilee year in 1916, the Suguna Vilasa Sabha undertook a final visit to Ceylon. According to Sambanda Mudaliar, it turned out to be a memorable occasion, since he was awarded the ‘Rao Sahib’ title as part of the king’s birthday honours. It was announced as part of a scene in their popular play Sabapathy. It was greeted with thunderous applause.
According to Kalaiarasu K. Sornalingam, a doyen of Tamil theatre in Ceylon, the Suguna Vilasa Sabha’s tours marked a turning point in the history of theatre in the island nation. Inspired by its performances, he founded the Lanka Subodha Vilasa Sabha in 1913, which in turn led to the formation of other troupes in places such as Jaffna. Sornalingam considered Sambanda Mudaliar his guru, and the latter, too, recognised him as an artiste of repute in his book Naan Kanda Naadaga Kalaignargal.
Sambanda Mudaliar’s influence as a theatre-personality truly transcended borders.

title: In Texas, a historic Route 66 neighborhood taps its deep roots for a revival
content:
In Texas, a historic Route 66 neighborhood taps its deep roots for a revival
Loading...
| Amarillo, Texas
David Rosas turns off Arthur Avenue and starts walking through the old Mexican American Barrio of his childhood.
The first landmark is an empty lot.
His grandmother’s house once stood here, Mr. Rosas says. It was a place where relatives streamed in and out, coffee seemed always to be brewing, and everyone came to learn the family news. He has called it the family’s “bank, library, meeting place.”
Why We Wrote This
Many American neighborhoods carry the history of the people who built them and helped them flourish. When time erodes the bonds that define a place, new energy can help a place like the Barrio in Amarillo, Texas, renew itself.
He remembers the railroad men walking home for lunch, then heading back to work. Afterward, his grandmother and a neighbor would pull out flour, water, and lard and begin making tortillas, the kitchen filling with the familiar rhythm of the rolling pins.
“I wish I could hear it right now,” he says. Walking down the street a few blocks, he passes a funeral home. But Mr. Rosas knows the building by an older name: El Salón Mexicano.
His grandfather, Mateo Lopez, a Santa Fe railroad worker, helped build the neighborhood hall with other residents in the 1930s as a place for dances, weddings, and quinceañeras. “The Barrio is a town within a town,” Mr. Rosas says. “We didn’t travel far.”
The short walk amounts to a century of Barrio history, a story about how American communities are made, and often remade in order to endure. In the late 19th century, Mexican railroad workers, brought in through programs of the Santa Fe Railway, arrived with their families and built homes, businesses, and a Catholic church – a world within a world, shaped partly by the segregation and discrimination that kept them apart from much of the city’s wider civic life. But the Barrio can be seen, too, as a recognizable American story of frontier towns in which neighbors helped out neighbors, and civic services became a fully communal affair.
Like so many small towns along Route 66, old boundaries have loosened, and families have scattered as regional economies reshape where people work and live. But the neighborhood is being rebuilt again. Their challenge is no longer how to create a community within those boundaries, but how to carry forward the belonging that grew there.
There is a Route 66 irony embedded in the Barrio’s story. Its 10th Avenue was part of the original highway in 1926 – the road Americans would celebrate as the “Main Street of America.” It was rerouted north in 1932.
Yet on the other side of Amarillo’s railroad tracks, Mexican American families kept building their version of the Main Street ideal: businesses, places to gather, familiar families, and a commitment to one another.
■ ■ ■
For Mr. Rosas, that older Main Street can be measured less in storefronts than in relationships.
“Back then when you met somebody, an elderly gentleman, they asked you who your parents were,” he says. He would give his name, and the older man would begin placing him.
Lupe’s son. Mateo’s grandson. Then would come the stories: Your father helped me with this. I knew your grandfather. “Being recognized by your parents and your grandparents, it’s a big deal,” Mr. Rosas says. “I mean, it carried weight.”
His grandfather was one of the first pillars of the Barrio. His father, Lupe Rosas, carried that ethic into a different era. A World War II veteran who later worked at Amarillo’s veterans hospital, he was one of the first members of the NAACP. In the 1950s, he and two Catholic priests conducted a sit-in at one of Amarillo’s whites-only restaurants.
Lupe also became one of the people neighbors sought out when they did not know how to navigate institutions beyond the Barrio. Someone needed help with a Social Security form. Someone had a problem with the city. Someone needed to know whom to ask.
“When people had problems, nobody had a lawyer,” says Mr. Rosas, who dropped out of school in the eighth grade and went on to spend four decades selling cars. “My dad could figure something out. And I do that for a lot of people.”
Mr. Rosas holds no public office. But neighbors call him when trash is not picked up or a dilapidated property becomes a problem. He goes to city meetings, pushes officials for neighborhood investment, and says Amarillo’s current mayor takes his calls.
People sometimes call him the “mayor of the Barrio.” Mr. Rosas has given himself an arguably grander title, printed on his business card: H.M.I.C. – “Head Mexican in Charge.”
His charm and levity, however, belie his seriousness. In 2017 he became part of a neighborhood revitalization process.
For him, the effort is about more than getting sidewalks or city money. His grandmother’s house is gone. Relatives have scattered across Amarillo and beyond. Mr. Rosas himself lives about five miles from the Barrio.
The old social geography is harder to see. “It’s getting lost,” he says.
■ ■ ■
Teresa Kenedy turns off Arthur Avenue onto 10th and drives slowly toward the railroad tracks, narrating the Barrio almost block by block.
There are the murals marking the entrance to the old neighborhood. Then the new trees. Banners celebrating Día de los Muertos with sugar skulls. Street lamps. Bike racks. Nine street benches painted in reds, blues, and greens. Most noticeably, there are sidewalks – wide, wheelchair accessible stretches of concrete in a neighborhood where, away from the businesses, sidewalks are scarce.
“What you’re seeing – none of that was here prior to April of this year,” says Ms. Kenedy, now the president of The Barrio Neighborhood Planning Committee, on which Mr. Rosas serves, too. For the old main street, it amounts to a $6.1 million makeover the organization helped facilitate.
But Ms. Kenedy does not describe the project as an attempt to make 10th Avenue look new. She talks instead about making the street announce where it is – and what came before.
For Mr. Rosas, the Barrio is an inheritance. He can walk its streets through generations of his own family. His argument for rebuilding the neighborhood begins with memory, but becomes a claim on the larger city: “We’ve paid taxes forever,” he says. “I want some of that money back here.”
Ms. Kenedy’s attachment is chosen. She did not grow up in the Barrio, but in tiny Snowville, Utah, near the Idaho state line, where hers was the only Hispanic family for about 20 miles. Her father died when she was age 2, leaving her mother to raise seven children. Ms. Kenedy says everyone chipped in; she began working at age 9, first as a babysitter and then as a dishwasher.
She arrived in the Amarillo area for college at age 20, studying to be a social worker, “connecting people with resources.”
Her biography appears almost geographically during the drive. She passes Caprock High School, where she worked for 13 years in drug prevention, and then Bowie Middle School, where she spent another seven.
Then she became the coordinator of a federally funded program to place the children of migrant farmworkers in school, even though they might remain for only weeks or months before their families moved on.
When she retired in 2015, Ms. Kenedy, a widow with no children, committed to volunteering in the Barrio, her home for over 45 years.
Together, she and Mr. Rosas represent the challenge facing the Barrio now. The first generations built a community from the ground up. Their descendants inherited its stories and obligations. The work of this generation is different: to turn that inheritance into something sturdy enough to survive change.
In 2018, Ms. Kenedy became something of the Barrio’s historian. She led a task force that interviewed older residents for a book that would preserve the neighborhood’s collective memory.
She conducted many of the interviews herself. When the group needed someone to turn the interviews into a book and nobody volunteered, Ms. Kenedy did that, too.
The book was also part of the committee’s effort to put together a historical map. The map and the memories fed into a neighborhood plan.
And the plan, eventually, became the trees, benches, and lights along 10th Avenue.
Memory, in other words, became infrastructure.
■ ■ ■
More than a century after an earlier generation built El Salón Mexicano because the Barrio needed somewhere to gather, Mr. Rosas and Ms. Kenedy are trying to create another such place – not to restore the confining boundaries of the old neighborhood, but to give its communal life a place to flourish again.
The group calls it La Plazita. Right now it’s an empty lot, but they are planning to turn it into a community park with a stage. Mr. Rosas was the one who spotted the property for sale. The city ultimately acquired it and deeded it to the planning committee.
For now, there is a mural, several benches, sponsored paving stones, and a storage building. Ms. Kenedy envisions a performance stage, food trucks, mariachi musicians, folklórico dancers, pop-up markets, movie nights, quinceañeras, and wedding receptions. There will be free Wi-Fi. The committee has already begun holding events on the unfinished lot so people will get used to coming there.
As she walks through the unfinished La Plazita, she also mentions the legacy of Mateo Lopez.
“Here’s someone who came as a young man with his wife from Mexico to the United States, came to Amarillo, helped build this railroad, helped build a community center – and his grandson is now helping renovate this neighborhood. It came full circle, right?”

title: People Of Purpose: How Prerana Founder Priti Patkar Reached 19,883 Children From Red-Light Areas Across Maharashtra
content:
For Priti Patkar, social work began not with a predetermined career path, but with a question that emerged from witnessing the lives of children growing up in Mumbai’s red-light areas: how could children born into exploitation be given the opportunity to choose a different future.
Trained as a social worker at Nirmala Niketan and later at the Tata Institute of Social Sciences, where she stood first in her specialisation, Priti’s understanding of child protection was shaped by her early exposure to Kamathipura. Her journey eventually led to the founding of Prerana, an organisation focused on protecting women and children from trafficking, commercial sexual exploitation and other forms of violence.
A Defining Encounter With Kamathipura
A visit to Kamathipura in 1986 became a turning point in Priti’s life. As a social-work student, she encountered children growing up amid circumstances where exploitation could continue across generations.
What stayed with her was three generations and the youngest of them being a child of women from the same family on the streets and bylanes of Kamathipura, soliciting for customers. The experience made her confront a difficult question: what could be done to ensure that children born into such circumstances were not automatically destined to inherit the same life?
At the time, children’s rights were receiving increasing attention globally, yet Priti saw how children in places like Kamathipura remained largely invisible while many of their basic rights were being violated.
That experience became part of the foundation for Prerana, which she began with her husband, Dr. Pravin Patkar, with support and guidance from Mrs. Farida Lambay and Dr. Hazel D’Lima.
From Rescue To Prevention
Priti’s early experiences also changed how she understood social intervention. She realised that protecting children could not simply mean removing them from immediate danger.
Children needed safe spaces, education, healthcare, counselling, family support and pathways towards a different future. This thinking led to the development of Prerana’s Night Care Centre programme, described in the interview as the first initiative of its kind.
The programme provided children born to women in prostitution with a safe place to stay during the night, away from the violence, exploitation and influences of the red-light area. But the intervention went beyond shelter. Children were supported with education, healthcare, nutrition and psychosocial care.
Prerana also worked with their mothers. The intention was not to separate mothers and children, but to protect children while recognising the importance of their relationships with their families.
For Priti, that distinction remains central. The goal was never to decide what a child should become. It was to create the conditions in which a child could eventually decide for themselves.
Challenging Stigma And Intergenerational Trafficking
The work was not without resistance. Priti recalls that there was widespread stigma surrounding children born to women in prostitution, including the assumption that they would inevitably enter the same trade as their mothers.
Prerana had to challenge both the circumstances surrounding these children and the assumptions society had made about their futures.
The organisation also encountered resistance from people benefiting from the sex trade, particularly when children were supported in making choices that could take them away from exploitation. Priti emphasises that rescue alone cannot protect a child from being trafficked again. Without safe environments, education, family and community support, rehabilitation and continued services, children can remain vulnerable to re-trafficking.
Its work with women similarly extended beyond immediate assistance. Prerana has supported access to alternative rehabilitation and livelihood opportunities, social-security entitlements, identity and protection documents, and government schemes and services.
The broader aim has been to strengthen people’s ability to make informed choices and become more independent.
Building Trust, Sharing Learning
For Priti, meaningful social change requires patience. Communities cannot simply be approached with an outside solution and expected to participate immediately. Trust has to be built over time.
Even in the early years, convincing mothers to send their children to Prerana’s Night Care Centres required demonstrating that the organisation was not trying to separate them from their children. It was creating a safe environment where children could be protected while their mothers worked.
Over time, Priti’s work also reinforced her belief that people closest to a problem must be part of its solution. Mothers, children and communities have shaped Prerana’s learning, while collaboration with government agencies, police, schools and other civil-society organisations has helped extend that learning.
She believes social change cannot belong to one organisation alone. Interventions need to be shared, documented and adapted so that successful approaches can reach more people.
Measuring Success Through Choices
For Priti, the success of an intervention cannot be reduced to the number of children reached.
Prerana looks at whether children remain safe, connected to education and supported in their health and psychosocial needs. It also follows individual journeys, including educational progress and barriers that can lead to children dropping out of school.
But there is another measure that matters deeply to her: whether a person’s choices have expanded.
The Night Care Centre, which has benefited thousands of children over the years, represents this philosophy. Some children have gone on to pursue higher education, find employment and build lives different from what society once assumed would be their destiny.
For Priti, that is the larger purpose of child protection. It is not simply about removing a child from a dangerous situation. It is about creating safety, support and opportunities so that the child can imagine and choose a future beyond the circumstances into which they were born.
The Logical Indian Perspective
Priti Patkar’s journey began with witnessing an uncomfortable reality in Kamathipura and asking what could be done differently. Her work with Prerana has since focused on a principle that runs through her approach to child protection: rescue can be only the beginning.
From creating safe spaces at night to supporting education, healthcare, rehabilitation and family relationships, the focus has remained on disrupting intergenerational exploitation without taking away a child’s agency.
Her experience also shows why lasting social change requires more than individual interventions. It demands trust, community participation, institutional collaboration and a willingness to learn from the people closest to the problem.
At the heart of Priti’s work is a simple idea: every child deserves safety, dignity and the freedom to decide what they want their life to become.

title: He taught himself traditional Teochew crafts as a boy. More than 40 years later, he's still learning
content:
He taught himself traditional Teochew crafts as a boy. More than 40 years later, he's still learning
Mr Francis Tan Kwee Chye began teaching himself traditional Teochew crafts at nine years of age, improvising with chocolate wrappers, scrap wood and a penknife. More than four decades later, he is still making, learning and trying to pass on a craft with a dwindling number of practitioners.
I had been in the living quarters of Sean Hua Zee Temple only for a few minutes, but I was already starting to sweat. Despite the afternoon heat, the ceiling fan remained off.
It couldn't be helped, though. In the middle of the room, Mr Francis Tan Kwee Chye was hard at work, carefully rubbing gold leaf into a wooden signboard. Turning the fan on for some cooling relief would blow the delicate foil away.
When I had arrived at the temple off Changi Road, which doubles as Mr Tan's home and studio, the 50-year-old welcomed me in before apologetically asking for a few minutes to finish the work in front of him.
As a master of traditional Teochew crafts, he's spent over three decades handmaking wood carvings, temple lanterns, paper effigies and even refurbishing deity statues.
Mr Tan is not especially talkative, but once the conversation turns to his work, he seems to light up. He readily reaches for photographs, old pieces or reference books, eager to explain how something was made or point out a detail that might otherwise escape my notice.
At one point during my visit, he even broke open a container that had been sealed for about two decades to show me the miniature figurines kept inside, some of which he had made in primary school.
Straightforward doesn't interest him – he prefers the challenge of elaborate flowers, birds and animals over simpler creations such as tables and chairs.
"I like to make special things," he said simply.
Presented with proof after proof of Mr Tan's artistry, I was surprised to learn that his impressive skills were almost entirely self-taught.
He has never formally apprenticed under a master, instead painstakingly honing his abilities through years of observation, failed attempts and fragments of guidance from other artists.
LEARNING WITHOUT A TEACHER
At first glance, Sean Hua Zee Temple looks like a regular home, wedged into the middle of a row of landed houses. A red banner and signboard beckon devotees in to make their prayers and offerings.
Growing up in a home temple made objects such as wood carvings and lanterns a familiar part of his surroundings. As a child, Mr Tan also often accompanied his mother to street opera performances. He understood little of what was being sung on stage, but was drawn to crafts used in the street opera that were similar to those displayed around the temples.
In Primary 3, Mr Tan started trying to reproduce some of them himself.
One of his earliest projects was a miniature joss paper dragon traditionally presented to deities during birthday celebrations.
With no YouTube or internet tutorials to consult back then, Mr Tan photographed a full-sized version with a camera, scaled down its proportions, then drew and coloured in the smaller version himself.
Proper materials were expensive for a nine-year-old, so he improvised. "Instead of buying gold foil, I used chocolate wrappers to get the same effect," he said.
By around Primary 6, Mr Tan had also started trying his hand at wood carving. Still aged only 12, Mr Tan would run out after school to nearby factories to ask for unwanted wooden pallets. He would break them down with a hammer himself and carry the usable pieces home.
Having no carving tools, he relied on a penknife, but the makeshift tool left his hands blistered, while mistakes were frequent. "When you first carve, you don't know how to control your strength," he said. "So it's either I cut it too deep or I scraped off the part which I wanted."
With no teacher to instruct him, he spent several months on his first wood carving: a sea lion. Even now, about 40 years later, he still keeps some of those early pieces to measure his progress – a physical record from a time when taking photographs was costly and mobile phones did not yet exist.
Mr Tan remembers his mother being "quite supportive, because I (wasn't) doing anything wrong or illegal". Nevertheless, he's aware that his dedication and persistence back then may have been seen as rather unusual by others, given his young age.
At around 15, Mr Tan joined a lion dance troupe. After a friend in the troupe mentioned his craft hobby to an events company they worked with, Mr Tan was invited to make miniature Chinese opera masks in front of tour groups as a live demonstration.
"I was young, so I felt quite excited that my work was being recognised," he recalled.
Despite that early recognition, Mr Tan never imagined that crafts would eventually become his livelihood.
A CRAFT THAT NEVER LEFT HIM
After his O-Levels, Mr Tan studied drafting at the Institute of Technical Education. After graduating, he worked as a draftsman for a few years before being unexpectedly retrenched. He later became a construction project coordinator at another company.
All the while, though, he found himself unable to set aside traditional crafts.
His construction boss allowed him to take discarded materials from work sites, so he continued taking on craft projects on the side, partly for extra income but also "because of passion".
At the same time, he struggled to find senior craftsmen to teach him to perfect the skills he'd already developed.
When Mr Tan was about 24, a relative who ran a joss paper shop asked him to refurbish a deity statue. Mr Tan turned him down because he didn't feel confident he could do the work.
His relative persisted, assuring him that a professional could take over if needed. Mr Tan agreed, and upon completing his refurbishment, his relative showed it to experienced craftsmen without revealing who had done it.
Mr Tan was present, allowing him a rare chance to listen to qualified critiques.
"I just sat there and listened to the feedback … just tried to improve from there."
About six years after that, Mr Tan approached a joss paper shop owner hoping to learn from him, but was turned away for reasons he never learnt.
With no one willing to teach him, Mr Tan has been honing his craft skills much as he did in childhood – by studying finished objects and, in a way, reverse engineering the techniques that went into creating them by himself.
Even today, his workspace is crowded with reference books on Chinese opera characters, costumes and traditional weapons to fill the gaps in his formal knowledge.
In his early 40s, Mr Tan concluded his career in construction, concerned about prolonged exposure to cement and sand dust. Having built up a small base of regular customers for his craft work, he decided it was time to make his part-time passion a full-time occupation.
AN OLD CRAFT IN MODERN SINGAPORE
Mr Tan's line of work is one that some people would rather keep at a distance. In his experience, some are reluctant even to touch joss paper or enter shops selling it because of the associations with the dead.
"But if you don't do it, who is going to do it? Somebody has to do this," he said.
For some customers, Mr Tan's creations serve a deeply personal purpose.
Several years ago, a couple approached him with an unusual request: Would he make them two joss paper replicas of the same portable handheld fan, each in a different colour?
The request was made through a third party, who told Mr Tan that the couple had dreamt of their recently deceased daughter asking for the fans, and wanted joss paper versions that could be burnt as offerings for her.
They had spent some time searching around Singapore and even making inquiries with Malaysia-based businesses, but no one seemed to be able or willing to take on their request.
He did not know much else – not even the couple's ages, nor how old their daughter had been when she died.
With only a photograph and no measurements provided, Mr Tan had to rely on online specifications for the fan's dimensions. After about six months of experimentation, he eventually made two fans out of joss paper. The customer had separately asked for a power bank and cable to accompany them.
Mr Tan admitted to having felt daunted at first. He had even suggested the parents simply buy real fans for about S$20 (US$15.80) each, rather than pay him much more to create joss paper replicas.
"After listening to their story, to me it's a motivation," he said. "It pushed me to make (the fans) more detailed, and try to make the deceased happy."
He has since gone on to recreate other contemporary objects out of traditional joss paper, including track shoes and dumbbells. Such customised orders often require extensive trial and error, so he takes them on only when he has time to spare.
"To me, it's a form of respect to the deceased," he said. "Try to make it as real as possible, even though it's a joss paper product."
After spending so much of his life in traditional crafts, Mr Tan said he is no longer uneasy about the trade's association with death. He sees it instead as a service to the deceased and, in turn, to the families commissioning the pieces, who may find some comfort in being able to fulfil a loved one's final or imagined wishes.
KEEPING TRADITIONAL CRAFTS ALIVE IN SINGAPORE
As much as Mr Tan struggled to find master craftsmen to learn from in his young adulthood, that struggle may be even greater for young learners today.
He said most traditional craftsmen in Singapore are already well into their 60s and older. And at the age of 50, he reckons he could be among the youngest of those still working today.
Two years ago, Mr Tan began conducting traditional craft workshops and found that many participants recognised the objects he showed them without knowing how they were made or what they meant. Among locals, older participants also tended to outnumber younger adults.
Some young people have nevertheless approached him wanting to learn directly from him, placing the self-taught craftsman in the unfamiliar role of potential teacher.
While Mr Tan is willing, he has yet to accept an apprentice. Showing interest alone is not enough for him.
"I'm still observing people. Before you teach someone, you have to see their character."
The challenges don't end there for the micro-industry of traditional Teochew crafts.
The already small pool of traditional craft makers and craft businesses is dwindling as older practitioners retire. The work also demands long hours and specialised skills, making it difficult to bring in temporary help during periods of heightened demand, such as the seventh month of the Chinese lunar calendar.
"You feel sad, but (you have) no choice," said Mr Tan.
At the same time, demand for handmade work is dipping in a sea of cheaper, ready-made alternatives easily available on e-commerce sites such as Shopee and Taobao. To less-informed customers, printed or machine-made products may look little different from handmade ones.
These days, it's not unusual for Mr Tan to spend up to a week making an item that sells for only about S$100.
Also at risk of disappearing are the rich history and knowledge behind these traditional artefacts – the symbolism and significance behind the colours, motifs and forms they bear, all of which Mr Tan has absorbed over decades of making them.
"It's art, but it's also connected with culture," he said. "After you do it for some time, you will understand more about Chinese culture."
By now, little separates Mr Tan's work from the rest of his life. Sean Hua Zee Temple is both home and studio, filled with tools, reference books and pieces accumulated over decades.
The craft was already part of that life when he met his wife through a dating service in 2013, while he was still working in construction. Before they married, he made clear what he did.
"I did tell her what I'm doing," he recalled. "If she accepts it, then we can get together. If she cannot accept it, then no choice."
Certainly, Mr Tan's trade may seem an unconventional one compared to the office jobs that dominate the job market today.
But Mr Tan said he prefers not to make such comparisons – nor does he appear to feel particularly isolated working in a small, shrinking trade. He's become accustomed to solving problems on his own, trying different ideas, materials or methods until something works.
It is far from the future Mr Tan imagined at nine, when crafts were simply a hobby. At 50, he now sees himself continuing for as long as his strength and eyesight allow.
"Maybe I'll just continue until the day I am not very fit to do this type of traditional craft."
If he has his way, even retirement won't part him from his art. Even after stepping back from work, he sees himself continuing to make paper crafts "as a memory, or just for myself".

title: How fake Naxos potatoes and modern ambitions are threatening the future of a world-renowned crop
content:
Historic Naxos potatoes hold protected status, but young people on the island no longer want to be farmers.
Naxos is the largest island in the Cyclades and its eponymous variety of potatoes has been grown here since the late 18th century. Sold all over Europe, the crop is an important part of the local economy. Sowing and harvesting takes place twice a year with the second time happening every September. Euronews went to meet Naxos potato farmers and learn more about a crop under threat.
We meet Stelios Vathrakokoilis, one of the biggest potato growers on Naxos and President of the Galanado Agricultural Cooperative, and ask him what makes the island’s potatoes so special. "First of all, we have abundant sunshine almost all year round," he says. "Second, we have the sea all around us, at a distance of three to four kilometres. Third, we use cow manure on our fields, as much as we judge necessary, and the fourth and most important factor is that our subsoil lacks certain elements. That element is calcium. If, in these areas, you grow tomatoes or vegetables without adding fertilisers, they will start rotting on the back side of the fruit. That means a lack of calcium. Potatoes are not bothered by this. So it is the absence of calcium from our soils that gives the potato about 80 per cent of its distinctive flavour."
Young people don't want to farm potatoes anymore
In the 1980s, annual production of Naxos potatoes reached 15,000 tonnes. Every member of a family worked on the crop. Families today are smaller and children follow other career paths. Some 300 families on the Cycladic island are involved in potato farming today and production has dropped to a mere 5,000 tonnes.
What is a fake Naxos potato?
In 2010, the Naxos potato was granted protected status. This means that potatoes must be given the seal of approval before being able to be sold under the Naxos potato label.
Farmer Stelios Vathrakokoilis explains that some package up potatoes as Naxos when they are, in fact, inferior varieties.
"We started marketing Naxos potatoes first through the AB Vassilopoulos supermarket chain. A year later, Sklavenitis came in very strongly, followed by all the chains, so that all this product was going straight onto supermarket shelves."
"But even there, some fraud takes place. I don’t know who, but certain people buy potatoes from other regions, even other continents, especially Egypt. They take them into their packing plants, package them and sell them as Naxos potatoes."
"This happens even more in the street markets. If you walk into a market with 20 or 30 stalls, you will see all of them claiming to sell Naxos potatoes. They are not from Naxos. Out of forty stalls, perhaps one or two sell the real thing. Everyone calls their potatoes Naxos because the price is higher and the taste better. The upshot is that consumers can find genuine Naxos potatoes in 99 per cent of cases only on supermarket shelves. Only there will they find them."
Water and labour shortages threaten the future of Naxos potatoes
The shortage of labour has become acute in recent years and is a serious concern for farmers - it is very difficult to find workers with the legal right to work.
Water shortages are also an issue. More residents and tourists on the island along with prolonged drought means water resources are spread much more thin.
Farmers have to buy expensive water from the municipality, supplied from desalination plants.
Farmer Stelios Vathrakokoilis is sounding the alarm for the future, seeing production shrink and problems multiply:
"The basic precondition for having production is manpower. A second point, and what I see when I look ahead over the next five to ten years, is that we will be searching with binoculars to find a farmer, not only on Naxos but across Greece."
"It makes no sense for one 'stremma' of land to leave €1,500 in a Dutch farmer’s pocket, €1,200 for an Israeli farmer and €50 for a Greek farmer. It can not go on like this! Clearly we are doing something wrong. We are still using traditional methods, techniques from decades ago, and we are not moving towards something different, such as hydroponics or similar systems, with smaller areas, better working conditions and more income."
"What I see is that in 5–10 years there will be no Greek farmers left anywhere in the country. And I think this is broadly a European issue as well, as we can see from the protests farmers are staging in France and Germany."
"It is not sustainable to pay €2.5 per litre for diesel fuel, to have fertiliser prices through the roof, seed prices through the roof and monthly wages of around €2,500. If you try to farm under these conditions, you will end up completely in the red," stresses Stelios Vathrakokoilis.
The local farmers union is trying to help
This year the Union of Agricultural Cooperatives of Naxos marks a century of activity. It stands by the producers and works to solve the many challenges facing the island’s agricultural and livestock sectors. The Union’s goal is to support both the product and the people who grow it:
"Naxos potatoes are not just another product. They are the history of the place, its production, its economy. They are the wealth of the farmer and the livestock breeder," Dimitris Kapounis, President of the Union of Agricultural Cooperatives of Naxos, tells Euronews.
"Potatoes arrived on Naxos before the time of Kapodistrias, so you can see the passion, the love, the genuine cultivation of the land in this chapter we call Naxos potatoes," he says.
Every year the island hosts a major festival celebrating the potato. The 17th Potato Festival was held on 12 September at the port of Naxos. The centenary of the founding of the Union of Agricultural Cooperatives of Naxos was celebrated at the same time.
More than 3,000 people took part in the event in Nikiforos Mandilaras Square, alongside local organisations and representatives of the farming community. Residents and visitors sampled different recipes in which Naxos potatoes took centre stage, and enjoyed performances by musicians and dance groups.

title: New York's Muslims reclaim their city 25 years after 9/11 attacks
content: Asad Dandia was eight when he watched the Sept 11, 2001 attacks on television at his Pakistani-immigrant parents’ home in New York. Then came the backlash — years of Islamophobia as Americans processed attacks that had killed nearly 3,000 people. There was anger, suspicion and worse. At 19, Dandia experienced a police informant posing as a friend to infiltrate his family home, part of a now-disgraced surveillance effort purportedly seeking to detect extremism. Today, though, the 33-year-old historian finds a New York transformed: one with its first Muslim mayor, public prayers in Times Square and new mosques rising across the city. Asad Dandia conducts a guided tour about Malcolm X in the Harlem area of New York on Aug 22, 2026. — AFP “Twenty-five years after 9/11, we mourn and we grieve what happened, and at the same time, we recognise that I am not responsible for what happened,” he told AFP. “I don’t deserve to be targeted for what happened, and I am as much of a New Yorker as anybody else in that respect,” said Dandia, who leads walking tours centred on the city’s Muslim communities. Islamophobia surged in the United States after the 2001 attacks in which militants hijacked airliners and flew them into Manhattan’s World Trade Centre and the Pentagon outside Washington. A fourth plane crashed into a Pennsylvania field after a passenger revolt. Muslims reported increased public assaults and harassment, and some stopped wearing visual markers such as hijabs in a bid to conceal their religion. Meanwhile, US authorities monitored Muslims by requiring thousands of men and boys to register with the government, leading to many being deported from the country. “Everyone was in such fear,” said Mohammed Razvi, a native Pakistani who founded the Council of Peoples Organisation non-profit to support Muslims in New York after 9/11. “We had gunshots fired in our neighbourhood by individuals who felt that we were responsible,” he added. Razvi said he started introducing himself as “Mo” after 9/11 to avoid the stigma he encountered when saying “Mohammad”. “Muslims trying to live the American dream were being blamed for something they had nothing to do with or even control,” he said. ‘Terrifying’ In New York, police began surveilling hundreds of Muslims as part of their counterterrorism strategy, often targeting people without evidence of wrongdoing. Dandia experienced this as a 19-year-old college student, when a young Bangladeshi man joined a mutual aid charity he had started. The pair grew close: sharing meals, playing sports and even sleeping at Dandia’s home. But seven months later, the man revealed that he was an NYPD informant sent to monitor Dandia and his community. “It was heartbreaking, but it was also terrifying,” he recalled. “My relationship with the world around me shifted underneath my feet.” After his ordeal, Dandia and rights groups won a landmark legal settlement that restricted the NYPD from launching similar surveillance programmes and established a watchdog to monitor the force. For Gadier Abbas, an attorney with the Council on American-Islamic Relations, the NYPD programme was the prime example of the “anti-Muslim hysteria” that followed 9/11. But today, Abbas said, “there is a lot of hope”. “You see American Muslims in every single walk of life, almost at every single level, and that’s a testament to the vibrancy of the community.” ‘Power’ New York will soon boast the largest mosque in the state — one of more than 100 added since 2001 in New York — while Muslims are a rising cultural and political force. Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who took his oath of office on the Holy Quran, has become the new face of American leftist politics. Still, Islamophobia persists in the city where around nine per cent of the population is Muslim. In March, a far-right influencer organised a “Stop the Islamic Takeover of New York City” rally outside the mayor’s residence. Meanwhile, a conservative senator has said Mamdani should be sent to Guantanamo Bay, the US detention camp best known for holding 9/11 suspects. Some relatives of September 11 victims have called for Mamdani — an avid supporter of Palestinian rights — to skip this year’s 9/11 memorial, while other families have defended the mayor. Dandia acknowledged Islamophobia had not disappeared, but he was optimistic about how far New York’s Muslim community has come. “I’ve seen the growth of our institutional power, but also the recognition by other New Yorkers who are not Muslim, that we are all part of this city together,” he said. “I think that’s really valuable because, you know, Rome was not built overnight, and it was not built by one person or one group of people. It was built by the community.”

title: Reed Dance preserves cultural heritage: KZN Acting Premier
content:
KwaZulu-Natal Acting Premier Thembeni KaMadlopha-Mthethwa says the Umkhosi Womhlanga or Reed Dance continues to play an important role in preserving the province’s cultural heritage.
She was speaking at the eMachobeni Royal Palace in Ngwavuma during the first ceremony of the annual event on Saturday. The second ceremony will be held at the eMashobeni Royal Palace in uPhongolo next weekend.
KaMadlopha-Mthethwa also paid tribute to the Zulu royal family for promoting unity through Zulu cultural traditions.
“When you look at the history of South Africa and everything politics, the only thing that is uniting people in South Africa is the Zulu culture. You find that when you look at His Majesty the King, different political parties, when you look at the tent, they were all there, in support of the King.”
