Au Mexique, la consommation de champignons hallucinogènes existe depuis des millénaires au sein des communautés indigènes. Mais la science s'intéresse de plus en plus à cette médecine ancestrale qui pourrait aider à traiter certains troubles mentaux.
- Publié le 13-09-2026 à 11h04
D'une main experte, Alejandrina Pedro Castañeda écarte délicatement les broussailles qui recouvrent le pied d'une fougère géante. La végétation est dense dans cette forêt qui recouvre la Sierra Mazateca, une chaîne de montagnes du sud du Mexique. Mais cette Mexicaine de 60 ans la connaît par cœur, elle est née et a grandi à Huautla de Jiménez, un village indigène perché dans ces montagnes habitées depuis des milliers d'années par la communauté mazatèque à laquelle elle appartient. "Regarde", murmure-t-elle soudain, "en voici un. C'est un champignon médicinal."
Du bout des doigts, elle dégage les feuilles qui le recouvrent partiellement, puis coupe sa tige d'un coup sec. Haut de cinq centimètres, sa couleur brune le rend presque invisible à l'œil amateur. "Celui-ci, on le surnomme derrumbe (éboulement en français), car il pousse sur la terre retournée par un glissement de terrain. C'est une espèce qu'on ne trouve qu'ici." Avec 53 espèces de champignons hallucinogènes recensées sur son territoire, le Mexique détient le record mondial et concentre 25 % de la diversité mondiale. Oaxaca, l'État mexicain où se trouve la Sierra Mazateca, abrite 27 espèces à lui tout seul.
Pharmacie naturelle
Alejandrina Pedro Castañeda est guérisseuse, une vocation qui lui a été transmise par sa famille. "Quand j'étais petite, quand on allait cueillir des champignons, on chantait et on récitait une prière pour le premier qu'on trouvait. Puis on communiait, c'est-à-dire qu'on le mangeait. Ensuite, on lui disait : montre-moi où sont tes frères. Ils nous guidaient alors jusqu'à leur famille."
Le peuple mazatèque se soigne depuis toujours grâce aux ressources naturelles qu'il trouve dans la forêt. "Nous n'avons pas de produits chimiques ici, pas d'hôpital, notre pharmacie vivante a toujours été la nature, nous l'utilisons pour prévenir les maladies, pour être en phase avec notre environnement, avec notre corps." Avec précaution, elle arrache une grande feuille d'arbre et enferme le champignon dans cette poche naturelle. "Un seul comme celui-ci ne suffit pas. Pour obtenir un effet, il en faut au moins dix comme ça." Elle le fera ensuite sécher, puis l'utilisera lors des cérémonies, ces rituels de guérison durant lesquels les champignons sont consommés sous supervision d'un guérisseur mazatèque.
Une nouvelle substance psychédélique
Alejandrina Pedro Castañeda n'avait que six ans lorsqu'elle a assisté à sa première cérémonie. C'était avec Maria Sabina, la célèbre guérisseuse mazatèque qui a fait connaître au monde le pouvoir des champignons psychédéliques. En 1957, le magazine américain Life publie un reportage sur Maria Sabina et ses cérémonies. Cette découverte intrigue, et de nombreuses célébrités, comme John Lennon, Jim Morrison ou encore Bob Dylan, voyagent dans la Sierra Mazateca pour connaître Maria Sabina et sa magie.
La consommation de champignons hallucinogènes se démocratise, mais en 1970, le gouvernement américain décide d'inscrire la psilocybine, leur substance active, dans la catégorie la plus restrictive de la législation fédérale sur les substances contrôlées. Le Mexique les classe à son tour parmi les substances psychotropes réglementées en 1984. "Depuis, la psilocybine et les champignons hallucinogènes sont considérés comme dangereux et nocifs, sans aucun potentiel thérapeutique ou médical, précise Rebeca Espinosa, psychiatre mexicaine qui s'intéresse à ces substances depuis plusieurs années. On ne peut donc même pas les étudier via la recherche scientifique au Mexique. Seules les communautés indigènes qui utilisent ces champignons dans leur médecine traditionnelle, comme les Mazatèques, peuvent les consommer."
Intérêt de la science
Rebeca Espinosa et d'autres chercheurs mexicains plaident pour autoriser l'usage des champignons hallucinogènes à des fins de recherche scientifique. Selon la psychiatre, de nombreuses études scientifiques avaient déjà mis en lumière les bénéfices de la psilocybine avant son interdiction, notamment sur certains troubles mentaux. Ces dernières années, la réglementation s'est assouplie aux États-Unis, ouvrant la voie à de nouvelles recherches. "Elles se sont concentrées sur les troubles dépressifs majeurs et l'anxiété associée au cancer ou à d'autres maladies terminales. Dans tous ces domaines, on a obtenu de très bons résultats", affirme-t-elle. La psychiatre s'appuie notamment sur un essai clinique publié en 2021 dans le New England Journal of Medicine, revue médicale de référence. "Des chercheurs ont comparé l'efficacité de la psilocybine à celle de l'escitalopram, l'un des antidépresseurs les plus prescrits actuellement. Après six semaines, 70 % des patients traités à la psilocybine présentaient une réponse au traitement, contre 48 % de ceux ayant reçu de l'escitalopram."
Vers une nouvelle réglementation ?
Ces résultats, comme l'ouverture réglementaire observée aux États-Unis, nourrissent chez Rebeca Espinosa l'espoir d'un changement au Mexique. Ces dernières années, plusieurs initiatives parlementaires ont tenté de faire évoluer le statut de la psilocybine au Mexique. En 2021 puis en 2023, deux propositions ont cherché à autoriser et encadrer son usage scientifique et thérapeutique, notamment contre la dépression et l'anxiété.
Restées sans suite, elles ont été suivies en janvier 2026 d'un nouveau projet visant à reconnaître son potentiel thérapeutique, tout en continuant de la classer parmi les substances présentant un risque pour la santé publique. Si ce dernier projet aboutit, le Mexique pourrait enfin renouer avec ses racines indigènes. En attendant, certains thérapeutes préfèrent orienter leurs patients vers ceux qui savent le mieux, c'est-à-dire les guérisseurs. "Les psychiatres et les psychologues m'envoient leurs patients qui souffrent d'anxiété, d'anorexie, de dépression… Quand ils viennent me voir, on parvient à régler ces problèmes, glisse Alejandrina Pedro Castañeda dans un sourire complice. "C'est ça la médecine du champignon."

title: Nambitha Ben-Mazwi: The ‘Morning Star’ rises
content:
Before Nambitha Ben-Mazwi became an actress, before Netflix, international film festivals, and the terrifying experience of discovering that millions of Germans were about to watch her perform in their language, there was a blind grandmother who could somehow see her perfectly.
Ben-Mazwi’s grandmother, Nanziwe Florence Ben-Mazwi, called her “my star”. Nambitha would tiptoe into her house trying to surprise her and, despite having lost her sight later in life, her grandmother would immediately know she was there — and she had to give herself over for inspection.
“She’d run her hands across my face,” Ben-Mazwi says. “Then she checked my nails and earrings (a lady never leaves the house without them). After that, my hair and outfit were interrogated. My father was instructed to take his daughter shopping twice a year so she could keep up with fashion.” It was an extraordinary act of seeing a child and boosting her confidence.
Ben-Mazwi’s first name on her birth certificate is Nokwezi — “bright morning star” — and her grandmother also gave her something more useful than good grooming. She gave a dark-skinned little girl, teased about her complexion, an armoury of self-esteem. Her grandmother, herself dark-skinned, rejected skin-lightening and taught Nambitha to regard her colour as a “secret weapon”, which explains the woman sitting opposite me now.
Ben-Mazwi, also known as Lady Nam, is celebrating 10 years as a professional actress this month with a party at Artistry in Johannesburg on September 23, supported by Moët & Chandon, for whom she has long been an ambassador. There will be family, friends, industry colleagues, fans, and a toast from fellow actor Thapelo Mokoena. But the real party trick will be a South African screening of Tatort: Könige der Nacht (Kings of the Night), in which Ben-Mazwi plays Moya Alemu, an undocumented African migrant living in Zurich.
If, like Ben-Mazwi when she auditioned, you don’t know what Tatort is, well, it’s like a German being cast in The Polygamist and discovering that, yes, South Africans have indeed heard of the local series.
The German-language crime franchise has been running since 1970. Ben-Mazwi says her episode, which premiered in Europe in May, became the second-highest-performing viewing in its current run. She says she landed the part before understanding how enormous the show was in that part of the world.
“I didn’t know how popular it was,” she says. “It was just a random show and I was drawn to the role.
When she started telling European friends what she was working on, they were “shook”: ‘You’re in a Tatort?’, they’d gasp, which shook her too. She remembers thinking: “What have I gotten myself into? Then I started getting sh*t scared.”
The production had searched across Europe and Britain for an actress to play Moya before well-known Hollywood Swiss-born director Claudio Fäh suggested looking in Africa. Ben-Mazwi auditioned, got the callback and landed the lead role.
Her preparation involved flights spent plugged into AI-generated pronunciations of her lines, recordings played repeatedly in the car and frantic revisions with the crew in the make-up truck. She credits co-stars Carol Schuler and Anna Pieri Zuercher with helping her through it, particularly Schuler, who took her under her wing with a reassuring: “I’ve got you.”
For Moya, the character, Ben-Mazwi went further. She researched migration routes, Mediterranean crossings, undocumented migrants, passports and the circumstances that might drive a woman from the Ethiopia-Kenya border to Switzerland. The character’s story arrives at an awkward political moment in Europe, where immigration is a hot talking point.
Some viewers inevitably complained about having an immigration story “shoved down our throats”. Far more, she says, responded emotionally to Moya. “I have a following of Germans now,” she laughs. Some fans have demanded autographs and one apparently became upset because she hadn’t replied quickly enough.
Soon European agencies approached her and she now has representation there. The experience also exposed something less positive. “Black characters are like tokens to some extent,” she says. “So we should write the stories ourselves — a German writer doesn’t know an immigrant’s actual history or story. People write from their own place of representation.”
If African actors want to become the heroes rather than supporting characters in somebody else’s version of Africa, she argues, African creatives have to become writers, directors and producers too.
Ben-Mazwi, who plans to write, direct and produce, took a circuitous route to acting. She was the straight-A child who did the sensible thing because it pleased her parents. She studied business science at UCT, completed her honours and entered corporate life. Acting belonged to childhood Eisteddfods, speech and drama, theatre, and the ads she did for pocket money while studying.
Her parents wanted her to get a “proper degree”, and looking back she can see why. “Get the degree,” she says. “Not just as something to fall back on.” Business science taught her to understand that an actor is also, whether they like it or not, a small enterprise with invoices, contracts, strategy and demanding emails. But, she says, the sensible life began making her miserable. “Corporate took over. I started to feel like I was going insane. Something was missing.”
A friend announced she was abandoning her parents’ expectations and moving to Florence to study design, then turned the question back on Ben-Mazwi: “I know where your heart lies. What about you?” She says that her friend doing something reckless made her own recklessness seem reasonable. She went to New York for two weeks, and stayed six months.
Away from parents, expectations and what she calls “the noise”, something clicked. “I rediscovered my passion and decided, I’m gonna do this.”
Back in Cape Town she took a job at Heart FM establishing its digital marketing department, while slipping off to auditions. Her first television role came in e.tv’s Traffic. She remembers how she felt after wrapping the show: “Oh sh*t, I’m done now. Love it. That’s me.”
In 2015 she packed her Mazda and moved to Joburg with her mother. Her early credits included Doubt for Mzansi Magic, Black Mirror for Netflix, and the film Madiba with Laurence Fishburne. Commercials paid the bills while she assembled her international showreel.
Acting was also in the family. Her late uncle was Winston Ntshona, the Tony Award-winning South African theatre giant whose creative partnership with Athol Fugard and John Kani helped change theatre history. He recognised the bug in his niece long before she knew it was going to be her career. “He was like, ‘I was waiting for you to come along’.”
Ten years later, she has had six Netflix credits, and names Linda in Savage Beauty as one of her most meaningful roles. Playing a lesbian character made her acutely conscious of the responsibility of representing lives other than her own. She sought advice from LGBTQ+ friends, including a couple whose wedding she’d witnessed, because she wanted to get beyond “playing” sexuality and towards playing a human being.
Representation isn’t theoretical to Ben-Mazwi. She’s seen what her own presence on screen means to dark-skinned girls. One young woman, she tells me, had been so relentlessly demeaned over her complexion that she had attempted suicide. “That’s the power of representation,” Ben-Mazwi says. “Stars like Lupita Nyong’o have given us all permission to see ourselves in our wonder and glory.”
It also feeds into #SheSpeaksByLadyNam, the women’s platform she started in 2018 with an intimate Women’s Day brunch at Montecasino. It grew from there, with conversations around self-esteem, darker skin tones, health, endometriosis and the business of the arts. The subjects tend to follow her own life: she goes through something, gets to the other side, and then creates a space in which other women can talk about it.
Stars like Lupita Nyong’o have given us all permission to see ourselves in our wonder and glory.
— Nambitha Ben-Mazwi
For all the celebration of an international career, Ben-Mazwi is candid about the precariousness of acting in South Africa. Jobs can be separated by long periods of doing nothing. She says she is still owed salaries from productions dating back two years and believes streaming platforms have transformed opportunities for local actors while exposing how poorly protected they are elsewhere in the industry. Which explains why the business science graduate never left the building.
She talks about producing, directing, writing — and maybe even returning to corporate life.
As for Hollywood, there’s a US manager and discussions about visas. But the old idea that a South African actor must relocate to Los Angeles to become internationally successful feels obsolete. Work travels now. So do actors.
Surprisingly, Ben-Mazwi also talks about slowing down: “I’m at a time in my career where I want to focus on, you know, other things.” She says she wants a family.
When I ask her to imagine her 20-year celebration in 2036, I ask about her projected three children. “My oldest, and twins,” she laughs.
One of her dream roles would be to play Nina Simone, but she says she isn’t ready — a candid admission from an actress celebrating how far she’s come. “Some roles require more wrinkles on the soul,” she says. “I need to have more life first.”
Right now though, there’s September 23. She says the anniversary isn’t intended as self-congratulation. She wants to thank the first producer who took a chance, the casting directors, journalists, brands, audiences, family and friends — “the village” that got her here. And, of course, part of that village is a blind woman running her hands over a little girl’s face, checking her earrings and telling her that she is a born star.
Ten years into the career her family once considered too impractical to pursue, Nambitha Ben-Mazwi has ended up being viewed by 7.18-million Europeans. Her grandmother knew it all along.

title: Ministra Rachel Barros visita Casa da Igualdade Racial de Contagem (MG)
content:
A ministra da Igualdade Racial, Rachel Barros, visitou, na terça-feira (15), a Casa da Igualdade Racial de Contagem, na Região Metropolitana de Belo Horizonte (RMBH). Inaugurado no último dia 10, o equipamento é o sexto do país e o segundo de Minas Gerais a integrar o projeto-piloto do Programa Mais Igualdade, do Ministério da Igualdade Racial (MIR).
Casa funciona como espaço de acolhimento, orientação e apoio especializado
A Casa funciona como espaço de acolhimento, orientação e apoio especializado à população negra, comunidades tradicionais e outros grupos atingidos pela discriminação racial e étnica. Entre os serviços previstos estão atendimentos psicológico, social e jurídico a vítimas de crimes raciais e outras violações de direitos.
Durante a visita, Rachel Barros foi recebida ao som de atabaque e berimbau pelo grupo de capoeira Eskiva Brasil. A atividade contou com a presença de representantes da Prefeitura de Contagem, do Conselho Municipal de Promoção da Igualdade Racial (Compir), de comunidades quilombolas, povos de terreiro, congados e reinados.
A unidade integra o Programa Mais Igualdade e o Sistema Nacional de Promoção da Igualdade Racial (Sinapir). O projeto-piloto contempla seis municípios: Fortaleza (CE), Rio de Janeiro (RJ), Pelotas (RS), Salvador (BA), Itabira (MG) e Contagem (MG).
Cinco eixos
As ações desenvolvidas na Casa da Igualdade Racial estão organizadas em cinco eixos. O primeiro é a justiça racial, voltado ao apoio às vítimas de crimes raciais e de outras violações motivadas por discriminação racial e étnica.
O segundo é a inclusão produtiva, que busca ampliar oportunidades de desenvolvimento pessoal e profissional, com prioridade para mulheres negras e jovens negros. Já o eixo de cultura e educação prevê atividades educativas e culturais, especialmente a partir de referências afro-brasileiras.
O eixo convivência comunitária tem como objetivo fortalecer vínculos sociais, identidade e pertencimento das comunidades atendidas. Por fim, a pactuação federativa busca ampliar a articulação entre União, estados e municípios na implementação de políticas públicas de igualdade racial.
O Ministério da Igualdade Racial define as Casas como equipamentos destinados à redução das desigualdades raciais e ao fortalecimento dos vínculos sociais e culturais da população negra e das comunidades tradicionais.
Em Contagem, a Casa está localizada na rua Manoel de Matos, nº 162, no bairro Central Park. O atendimento é gratuito e ocorre de segunda a sexta-feira, das 8h às 17h.
Diálogo com povos tradicionais em Belo Horizonte
Também na terça-feira (15), o Ministério da Igualdade Racial promoveu um encontro com povos e comunidades tradicionais de Minas Gerais no Centro Nacional de Africanidade e Resistência Afro-brasileira (Cenarab), em Belo Horizonte.
O encontro reuniu representantes de povos de terreiro, comunidades quilombolas, reinados e congados. Durante a atividade, os participantes apresentaram demandas ao ministério e destacaram necessidades relacionadas à proteção dos povos tradicionais.
Além do momento de escuta, foram entregues reconhecimentos a pessoas e trajetórias ligadas à preservação da ancestralidade africana e à luta pela igualdade racial.

title: Fiction: A low-caste woman in Tamil Nadu’s Tranquebar is introduced to Christianity in 18th century
content:
Pecchi could not have guessed that the parangi who was leading her to this strange place was Schwartz – a man whose footsteps would later leave wide imprints on the soil of Thanjavur, whose name would one day be whispered as the shepherd of a new faith. For nearly 40 years, since Bartholomaeus Ziegenbalg had planted the first fragile seed of the Lutheran Mission in Tranquebar, Christianity had tried to push its tender roots into the hard earth of the south. The missionaries came from Denmark and Halle, carrying their strange books and stranger hopes – hoping to “rescue the heathen from darkness, to nurse their souls into salvation.”
But the land was old, its gods older still. The missionaries soon discovered that the people here clung fiercely to their pantheon, like children clutching the many fingers of one mother.
It was only with Schwartz’s arrival that the mission felt a new wind fill its sails.
Pecchi walked behind Schwartz towards the great doorway of the New Jerusalem Church, and a faint shiver passed through her. It was not entirely fear, nor entirely wonder, but something born of the two – like standing close to the sea at dusk, unsure whether to step back or forward.
“Have you been inside before?” he asked.
She shook her head, eyes moving slowly along the vastness of the structure.
It dawned on her that the parangi and his group were preaching a new religion, and she was entering a temple of this new faith. She had seen the temple at Godhanamangalam from outside. It looked large. She did not know much about the gods resident in the temple. Kadamban had said they were powerful gods, but they understood only the language of the Brahmins; Muthalamman was the goddess assigned to their caste. But Kadamban wasn’t happy with Her. Either She wasn’t as powerful as the Brahmin gods or didn’t take Her job seriously. Why else would they have to struggle for a living whilst the upper caste didn’t?
Now, faced with the enormous stone ribs of this church, the old temple seemed suddenly small, almost shy of its own shape and size.
After Bernt, Pecchi was no longer uncomfortable with white men, but this religion was strange. Rumours stirred in her memory – that parangis mocked the village gods, ate beef, drank liquor by the barrel and never washed after defecation. Yet, no rumour could explain the gentleness with which this white man placed a hand on her shoulder.
“My name is Schwartz,” he said. “You are safe here. This is God’s house.”
But she could not shake off her unease.
“My husband…” she began, “will you find out when he returns? He left five days after the Purattasi full moon.”
“We shall try,” said Schwartz. “First, you must eat.”
The moment he mentioned food, the world inside her collapsed into its oldest need. Fear, doubt, memory – all these could wait; hunger could not.
Just as she and Muthu received a cup of kanji and a sliver of fried fish, a woman hurried up to Schwartz, breathless in panic.
“Pastor! A pregnant woman – suddenly in labour – something is wrong.”
Schwartz’s voice was soft but firm. “Mariam, under the eye of the Lord, no one remains forsaken.”
“She cannot be moved,” Mariam insisted.
“Then you must help her, and we shall pray.”
Pecchi felt her fingers twitch – the instinct rising like a buried memory.
“I‒I can help,” she said timidly. “I am a maruthuvacchi.”
Schwartz turned to her with gratitude that warmed the cold air of the church.
“God indeed sends His servants at the right hour.”
The labour was long and dangerous. The baby pressed downwards too early; the mother’s breath trembled like a lamp flame. Pecchi’s hands moved steadily, though fear gnawed at her – fear of failure, fear of her ill luck. Between contractions, she whispered prayers to Muthalamman. She worried if the White God at the church would take offence at her calling her goddess. Would there be a clash between the gods? She didn’t know.
After hours of sweat and trembling effort, the newborn’s cry cut through the room – a perfect, unbroken flute. The mother’s exhausted smile glowed faintly in the lamplight.
For Pecchi, it felt as if a window had opened in her life and a soft wind had entered.
“You are blessed in your work,” Schwartz told her, his voice full of relief. “Truly, the Lord’s servant.”
Her heart brimmed with a pride she had not known in years.
“You haven’t had anything to eat! Will you please have your kanji?” Schwartz asked. Muthu wore a contented look, having had her meal.
Schwartz waited until she had eaten and then spoke gently: “If God has given you such hands, should they not serve the poor, serve His flock?”
Pecchi didn’t understand.
“I am asking if you’d want to work as a maruthuvacchi at the church?” he said.
“But I haven’t learned enough,” Pecchi said modestly.
“You could learn from a senior siddha vaidyar. The church will arrange that. You could work in our medical room,” said Schwartz.
So, she had found work; therefore, food.
Pecchi instantly promised Muthalamman two bottles of liquor. She had to find a way to settle her escalating dues.
The apothecary was a retired Dutch sailor who used vinegars and herbs with European names. The locals weren’t impressed. Some prescriptions went right against traditional wisdom. People were appalled that he should be prescribing a chalk mixture with opium, considered poison, to treat loose motion.
Samuel Benjamin Cnoll, a German scholar of palm-leaf texts, had been urging Schwartz to find a native healer. “The land already knows its cures, we must learn from them,” he had said.
A healer for women’s diseases would be a good start, Schwartz felt. That would bring in the female crowd. Women always seemed to want more from the gods than men.
So Pecchi joined the small medical hut beside the church. She inhaled foreign scents, ran her fingers over jars of rose-hip syrup and lavender balm, learning their temper as she matched them with the leaves and roots she had known since girlhood. Soon she was blending potions of her own, a union of western mixtures and forest remedies, and mothers began to arrive – women who trusted another woman’s ear, another woman’s hands.
Muthu, quick and eager, began to assist: crushing herbs, carrying warm water, wiping wounds with a tenderness that reminded Pecchi of her own mother. Mariam occasionally came to help; she had many other things to do.
Excerpted with permission from The Grammar of Silence: Five Centuries. Three Women. Towards Liberation, R Seshasayee, Rupa Publications.

title: Feira da Reforma Agrária tem Linn da Quebrada, Sarah Sampp e blocos de carnaval em BH
content:
Durante três dias, de 11 a 13 de setembro, a Serraria Souza Pinto, no centro de Belo Horizonte, será espaço de comercialização de alimentos, encontro, formação e cultura. Em sua sexta edição, a Feira Estadual da Reforma Agrária de Minas Gerais traz para a capital a produção das famílias acampadas e assentadas do Movimento dos Trabalhadores Rurais Sem Terra (MST) e uma programação cultural que aproxima campo e cidade.
A programação abre espaço para diferentes expressões da música brasileira e latino-americana. Entre os nomes de destaque estão: Linn da Quebrada, Sarah Sampp Maurício Tizumba, Sérgio Pererê e Rubinho do Vale. Como explica o MST, a Feira apresenta a Reforma Agrária Popular como um projeto de país, articulando produção de alimentos saudáveis, agroecologia, defesa da natureza, soberania alimentar, cultura popular e organização do povo.
“A cultura é parte da luta pela Reforma Agrária Popular. Da música de raiz ao rap, dos tambores ao carnaval, diferentes linguagens ocupam a cidade para celebrar os territórios, os saberes populares e a construção de um Brasil soberano”, destaca o movimento.
Programação Cultural
Na sexta-feira (11), o evento tem início com a Noite Anti-Imperialista. A abertura é às 20h30, com Maurício Tizumba, seguida pelo Festival Internacionalizemos a Esperança, com Giancarlo Borba, José Delgado, Nádia Campos, Paula Ferré, Cecilia Concha-Laborde e Sol Bueno.
No sábado (12), o Festival Terra, arte e pão celebra a diversidade da música mineira, com Mina Flor e Zé Pinto, Sérgio Pererê, Titane, Wilson Dias, Rubinho do Vale, Maria do Juá, Paiol de Tonha, Surubim e os Pocomãs e Tambores do Mucuri.
Já no domingo (13), o evento se encerra com o Beat da Terra, reunindo artistas da cena urbana e periférica. O destaque é Linn da Quebrada, que se apresenta às 20h30. A noite também terá Sarah Sampp, às 18h, e Imane Rane, às 19h. Mais cedo, o domingo terá uma programação diurna com Samba da Nossa Terra, Brota na Feira e o encontro do Bloco Pisa Ligeiro com Oficina Tambolelê e Filhas de Gaby.

title: The Missing Colors of Black American Pigment-Making
content:
The Missing Colors of Black American Pigment-Making
George Washington Carver is remembered as an innovative agricultural scientist, but his overlooked artistic work places him in a lineage of Black American natural dyeing traditions.
This article is part of a series focusing on underrepresented craft histories, researched and written by the 2025 Craft Archive Fellows, and organized in collaboration with the Center for Craft.
As one of humanity’s oldest crafts, natural pigment-making occupies the intersection of science, agriculture, and art. It requires curiosity and ingenuity to see a marigold flower, for instance, and know that it can stain fabrics with beautiful shades of mustard yellow to gold; to know, as our ancestors did, that they also have anti-microbial and anti-inflammatory properties. The blue color of denim traces its roots to indigo, a dye crop cultivated and processed by West Africans and their descendants throughout the Atlantic world. The global indigo trade that made blue textiles possible was deeply intertwined with enslaved labor and African dyeing knowledge.
Indigo is just one of many plant and mineral dyes that Africans and Black Americans have cultivated and used to create an array of colors. Bògòlanfini, also known as mudcloth, is one such earth-based color tradition dating back to the Bambara people during the 12th century in present-day Mali. The word itself describes the process: “Bògò” means “clay” or “mud,” “lan” means “by way of,” and “fini” means cloth in Bambara — “mud by way of cloth.”
Despite its foundational role in art and everyday life, natural pigment-making remains largely absent from institutional craft archives. As a researcher and environmental designer, I am deeply invested in Black people’s relationships to plant dyes, sustainable materials, and natural fibers. Yet, in searching for these histories, it seems that the archives fail to fully document the depth and breadth of this knowledge. What I found instead reminds us that pigment-making is an environmental craft tradition worthy of preservation, study, and contemporary revival.
Chemical-derived dyes were discovered accidentally in 1856, though plant-based dyes continued to be used well into the 20th century. Before then, the colors of textiles, art, and painted surfaces relied on natural dyes and pigments from local ecologies. Why do we celebrate finished works while overlooking the craft traditions — and people — that produced their color?
Despite the histories of plant dyes and pigments, I have not found any archives devoted specifically to natural color-making by Black folks in the United States. What I did find was that a celebrated historical figure’s pigment-making was one of his many great achievements, yet is often overshadowed by his other scientific contributions.
George Washington Carver is widely remembered as an innovative agricultural scientist whose research transformed Southern farming through crop rotation, soil restoration, and resource conservation. Born into slavery in Missouri in the early 1860s, Carver was motivated by a desire to support poor Black farmers still living with the economic devastation of slavery and sharecropping. He believed that scientific knowledge and creative practice should be accessible to everyone.
While Carver’s scientific accomplishments are well documented, his artistic and material practices have received far less attention. He was an accomplished artist, craftsperson, and natural pigment maker who understood resourcefulness as both necessity and a way of life. He believed people could make use of the materials available around them. As he notably advised, "From what you have, make what you want." One of the few moments when Carver's artistic work received widespread recognition came in a November 1941 Time magazine profile that described him as the "Black Leonardo." The article coincided with the opening of the George Washington Carver Museum and Archives at Tuskegee University and noted that the institution housed 71 of Carver's original paintings, many created with paints he and his assistant made from peanut oil, Alabama clay, and vegetables.

title: This Red-Ant Chutney Has Different Names Across India. Gordon Ramsay Just Put It in the Spotlight
content: In June 2026, Jharkhand Tourism shared a social-media video of Gordon Ramsay tasting the state’s red-ant chutney, describing his reaction as “absolutely delicious”. The clip brought fresh attention to a food that may look unusual to an outsider but has long been part of Indigenous diets across eastern, central and northeastern India. For communities living around forests in Jharkhand, Odisha, Chhattisgarh, West Bengal and Arunachal Pradesh, the red weaver ant is not something encountered as a culinary dare. It can be food, a seasonal forest resource, a traditional medicinal ingredient and, in some places, something that can be sold in local markets. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Jharkhand Tourism (@jharkhandtourism) And there is no single red-ant chutney. The same species appears in different food traditions, carrying different names, recipes and meanings depending on where you are. The ingredient is the red weaver ant, Oecophylla smaragdina. Demta and Hau in Jharkhand In Jharkhand, red-ant chutney is known by local names including Hau, while Demta is also used in some communities. The ants and their eggs are collected from tree nests and prepared with ingredients such as chillies, salt, garlic, ginger and coriander. The chutney is eaten with everyday foods rather than reserved as a novelty. Local accounts describe it being served with maaru-bhaat, puffed rice and vegetables. Bastar has its Chapda Travel west into Chhattisgarh, and the preparation takes another name. Red-ant chutney is particularly associated with Gond communities and is commonly known as Chapda, Chhapra or Chapura, depending on the locality. A 2024 review in Nature journal, “Bio-economic potential of ethno-entomophagy and its therapeutics in India,” documents the consumption of red ants among tribal communities in Chhattisgarh and notes that red-ant chutney is popular among Gond communities. The same review records red ants being consumed across several districts of Odisha, including Koraput, Kandhamal, Keonjhar, Sundargarh and Mayurbhanj. They may be roasted, eaten with rice, or fried with salt, chillies, spices and mustard oil. Bengal has Kurkut The tradition becomes particularly interesting when it reaches Jhargram in West Bengal. A 2020 study titled “On the Use of Red Ant Oecophylla smaragdina by the Indigenous People of Binpur, Jhargram, West Bengal,” by Atanu Mitra, Angsuman Chanda and Srimanta Kumar Raut, documented the practice in the Purnapani and Jorum forests of Binpur. The researchers had been visiting tribal settlements in the area since 1994, documenting how local people collected, prepared and used ants. Here, the red weaver ant is locally called Kurkut. What looks like one dish from a distance is actually a network of regional food traditions shaped by forests, seasons and local knowledge. Photograph: (IndiaToday) The study found that Indigenous people collected the ants and larvae between September and February, when large numbers of nests could be found in trees. The insects were used as food, medicine, and a commercial product. The recipe offers another glimpse of how local knowledge changes with geography. Researchers recorded a chutney made by grinding the ants with chilli, mint, onion, ginger, garlic, cumin, mustard oil and salt. Another preparation involved pounding the ants with onion, chilli, mustard oil and salt. It was eaten with rice for two or three days. Some families also boiled the ants and ate them directly. In Mayurbhanj, it is Kai In Mayurbhanj, Odisha, the red weaver ant is known as Kai, and the preparation is Kai Chutney. Here, the tradition has received formal recognition. On 2 January 2024, Similipal Kai Chutney of Odisha received a Geographical Indication registration. The official Intellectual Property India database lists the Mayurbhanj Kai Society Limited as the applicant and records the product as a registered food product from Odisha. Further east, it is Tonge and Babuk The tradition does not end in eastern India. In Arunachal Pradesh, Oecophylla smaragdina is one of the preferred edible insects among tribal communities. The ant is locally known by names including Tonge and Babuk, and both adult ants and larvae are consumed. One ant, several food cultures Put these regions together, and the map looks different. Hau or Demta in Jharkhand. Chapda in Chhattisgarh. Kai in Odisha. Kurkut in Jhargram. Tonge or Babuk in Arunachal Pradesh. The clip brought fresh attention to a food that may look unusual to an outsider but has long been part of Indigenous diets. Photograph: (Image enhanced with AI) The names change. So do the recipes and the communities that prepare them. What remains is the red weaver ant and a body of knowledge about collecting it, preparing it, and using it. That brings the story back to Gordon Ramsay. His reaction makes for a compelling social-media moment. But for generations, Indigenous people have known where these ants build their nests, when they are available, how to collect them, and how to turn them into food. Sources: ‘On the use of red ant Oecophylla smaragdina by the indigenous people of Binpur, Jhargram, West Bengal’: By Atanu Mitra, Angsuman Chanda and Srimanta Kumar Raut, Published in 2020 ‘Nutritional and anti-nutritional composition of Oecophylla smaragdina (Hymenoptera: Formicidae) and Odontotermes sp. (Isoptera: Termitidae): Two preferred edible insects of Arunachal Pradesh, India: By Jharna Chakravorty, Sampat Ghosh, Karsing Megu, Chuleui Jung, V.Benno Meyer-Rochow, Published on 2 July 2016 ‘If you are protein deficient, then definitely eat the chutney of 'Demta Ants', it not only tastes good to the tribals but also takes care of their health’: By Ravi Sinha, Published on 18 November 2022

title: 25 Years After September 11th, New York City Changed the Way We Prepare for Disasters
content:
This post was originally published by the National Center for Disaster Preparedness.
Twenty-five years after September 11th, 2001, it is still difficult to contemplate what happened without first thinking about the people. The firefighters and police officers who ran toward the World Trade Center, the emergency managers and health professionals trying to make sense of an unconceivable situation, the transit workers helping people evacuate Lower Manhattan, and the countless New Yorkers who simply tried to help one another are part of the city’s history. For those of us who work in the disaster risk management sector, September 11th is also a marker in the history of how we prepare, respond, and recover. The attacks exposed serious weaknesses in information sharing and coordination, but they also demonstrated an aspect of equal importance: when a disaster overwhelms an entire system, disaster survivors and organizations need to find ways to collaborate that may not have existed before the disaster began.
One of the most distinct ways to understand how dramatically the field has changed is to consider the technical tools emergency managers had available to them in 2001. New York City was already using geographic information systems (GIS), and these digital maps became enormously valuable during the response and recovery. However, transferring large digital files across networked systems was constrained by limited bandwidth, slower network speeds, and substantially less mature data infrastructure than emergency responders have access to today. Internet capacity was so limited that critical GIS disk drives had to be delivered daily by state troopers from offices in Albany to New York City so they could be used in the response. There were no smartphones, no social media, and no cloud-based systems through which responders could immediately share information or communicate with the public. Today, satellite imagery, digital maps, mobile communications, real-time data and increasingly sophisticated analytical tools are so commonplace that it can be easy to forget how innovative and useful they would have seemed on September 11th.
The communications problems that morning were not simply a matter of having cumbersome technology tools. The destruction of infrastructure in Lower Manhattan, combined with the extraordinary volume of people trying to communicate, overwhelmed telephone, cellular, and radio systems. Responders lost contact with colleagues and leadership and, critically, did not always have the information they needed about what was happening inside the towers. In the middle of an emergency, information can be as critical as any physical resource, yet it only becomes useful when it can move between people and organizations. This lesson helped change emergency management for the better. Since September 11th, New York City and other jurisdictions have invested heavily in interoperable communications, emergency operations centers, GIS, mass notification, mutual aid, regional planning, and training programs that bring agencies together to practice before a disaster occurs. We have become much more aware that a major disaster in New York is never the responsibility of a single agency.
Perhaps the most important change, however, has been cultural. Emergency management has become much more focused on relationships among organizations and on the ability to adapt to emergent events. The people responding to September 11th were not unprepared; many were among the most highly trained public safety professionals in the U.S. Instead, they were confronting something for which there was no precedent. The lesson was not that planning had failed, but that no plan can anticipate every scenario. Good preparedness therefore means creating organizations that can recognize when their assumptions are wrong, share information quickly, request assistance, and adapt. Contemporary training exercises are most valuable when they expose those unnerving moments when a plan breaks down, and responders have to figure out together what to do next.
A new generation of leaders has also developed professionally in the years since September 11th. Many of today’s emergency managers, public safety officials, hospital managers and disaster researchers began their careers around that time or were shaped by its aftermath. They have subsequently dealt with hurricanes, floods, wildfires, pandemics, infrastructure failures and other emergencies that have reinforced the same primary lesson: disasters cross boundaries. A hospital may depend on the electric grid; a transit system may determine whether people can reach safety; a private company may control infrastructure essential to public response; and community organizations may know things that government agencies cannot fathom from an emergency operations center. The strongest response is therefore rarely about one institution having all the answers. It is about people knowing whom to call, trusting one another, and being willing to share what they know.
We should be proud of how far this evolution has taken us, but we should also be cautious to assume that progress means we are prepared for everything. That’s far from true. The U.S. remains vulnerable to unprecedented disasters that could overwhelm the systems we have built, and preparedness requires sustained attention even when the immediate crisis has passed. Changes in federal priorities, programs and policies can also create uncertainty for state, local, Tribal, and territorial emergency managers who are trying to plan years ahead. At the same time, technology is moving faster than many of our public institutions. Artificial intelligence, remote sensing, automated damage assessments and predictive modeling may dramatically improve our ability to understand a disaster as it unfolds, but such digital tools cannot replace leadership or trust. A sophisticated system is of limited value if the people who need to use it do not adequately communicate with one another.
Twenty-five years later, I think that is one of the most important lessons we should carry forward. We cannot know what the next catastrophic event will look like, and the technologies available to us in another 25 years may be difficult to imagine today. What we can do is continue learning from experience, investing in systems that let credible information flow freely, and developing leaders who know how to collaborate and build relationships before they are needed. The greatest homage to the people who responded on September 11th is not to just remember what they did that day. It is to use what we learned from their experience to make the next response more effective. New York City has spent 25 years doing exactly that, and the work is not finished.
Thomas Chandler is a senior research scientist and the director of the National Center for Disaster Preparedness.

title: Lalbaugcha Raja: How a broken market and a vow created Mumbai’s iconic Ganpati
content:
Mumbai’s most famous Ganpati did not begin with a grand pandal or celebrity crowds. Its story began with a market that had shut down, families worried about their livelihood and a promise made to Lord Ganesha. In 1934, that promise took the form of an idol. More than nine decades later, Lalbaugcha Raja remains one of Mumbai’s most powerful symbols of faith and community.
When a market disappeared, so did livelihoods
In 1932, a market near Peru Chawl in Lalbaug was shut down. The closure affected vendors, traders and fishermen, including members of the local Koli community who depended on the area for their livelihood.
The community wanted a permanent marketplace. They prayed for a place where they could continue their trade. Their wish was eventually fulfilled when land was made available for a permanent market, which became the present Lalbaug Market.
A vow became Lalbaugcha Raja
The community’s gratitude became a religious promise, or navas. In September 1934, the traders and fishermen installed a public
Ganesha idol dressed in the traditional attire of a fisherman.
The Lalbaugcha Raja Sarvajanik Ganeshotsav Mandal was established in 1934. The idol soon became associated with the idea of a Navsacha Ganpati, or Ganesha believed to fulfil devotees’ wishes.
That origin gives the festival a meaning that goes beyond spectacle. At its heart is a very ordinary human hope: finding work, stability and a place to belong.
The Kambli family gave the Raja his familiar face
The idol’s distinctive form has another remarkable story. The Kambli family has been making the Lalbaugcha Raja idol since 1935, when Madhusudan Donduji Kambli began the tradition. Three generations of the family have since carried the work forward.
In 2011, Kambli Arts secured intellectual-property protection for the traditional design, after replicas of the famous idol became increasingly common.
So the Raja seen today is not simply a yearly sculpture. It carries a recognisable artistic tradition that has been carefully passed down.
Why millions still stand in line
The scale of Lalbaugcha Raja today is almost difficult to imagine. The idol is widely reported to attract around 1.5 million devotees a day during the festival.
There are separate arrangements for Mukh Darshan and Charan Sparsh or Navsachi darshan. Long queues, sometimes stretching for many hours, have become part of the Lalbaug experience.
The Maharashtra Tourism Department describes
Ganesh Chaturthi as a festival that brings together devotion, culture and community life. Lalbaugcha Raja is perhaps one of Mumbai’s clearest examples of that idea.
92 years completed, 93rd year begins
The mandal is celebrating its 93rd year in 2026, with the festival running from September 14 to September 25.
There is, however, one detail often missed in retellings of the story. The annual celebration was not literally held without interruption. In 2020, the mandal cancelled its traditional festivities during the COVID-19 pandemic and instead focused on awareness activities.
That interruption does not weaken the story. If anything, it makes the history more human. Lalbaugcha Raja began with people asking for a livelihood, survived generations of change and continues to bring strangers together every Ganesh Chaturthi.
Disclaimer: Historical accounts of Lalbaugcha Raja contain traditional narratives alongside documented records. Details such as the navas and its wish-fulfilling reputation reflect community belief and should not be treated as independently verifiable supernatural claims.

title: 10 iniciativas indígenas de retomada do território
content:
Em diferentes regiões do Brasil, povos indígenas têm recuperado terras transformadas em pastagens, degradadas pelo garimpo ou usadas como depósito de lixo, assumindo também o trabalho de restaurar a vegetação e restabelecer as condições para viver nesses lugares. São comunidades que avançam na direção contrária à das frentes de destruição: em vez de se limitarem a defender o que resta, passaram a lutar para retomar aquilo que foi perdido.
Destacamos aqui 10 reportagens publicadas pela Mongabay sobre como diversos povos indígenas do país, aliando tecnologia e saberes ancestrais, estão transformando seus territórios em lugares melhores para se viver.
Por que os Maxakali estão convocando os espíritos para recuperar a Mata Atlântica
Confinados em pequenas terras indígenas tomadas por pastagens no nordeste de Minas Gerais, os Tikmũ’ũn/Maxakali estão recuperando áreas de Mata Atlântica e implantando quintais agroflorestais por meio do projeto Hãmhi. Iniciada em 2023, a iniciativa forma e remunera agentes agroflorestais e viveiristas indígenas. O trabalho busca enfrentar a fome e recompor a vegetação necessária à vida cultural e religiosa do povo. A floresta é o lugar onde vivem os yãmĩyxop, povos-espíritos cujos cantos preservam o conhecimento sobre uma Mata Atlântica que já quase desapareceu na região.
Povo Xokleng restaura araucárias sagradas em terra indígena de Santa Catarina
Zág é como os Laklãnõ/Xokleng chamam a araucária — árvore para eles sagrada, cujas florestas hoje se reduzem a menos de 3% da área original. Vendo sua identidade desaparecer junto com esse ecossistema característico do Sul brasileiro, uma família da Terra Indígena Ibirama-Laklãnõ, em Santa Catarina, iniciou um projeto de restauração das araucárias. Desde então, a iniciativa já produziu mais de 140 mil mudas e reflorestou cerca de mil hectares. A iniciativa é uma resposta a um longo histórico de confinamento territorial dos Laklãnõ/Xokleng — da expulsão do Vale do Itajaí à construção da Barragem Norte.
Abolir as cercas, libertar a vida: povo Akroá Gamella retoma território ancestral e desativa lixão a céu aberto
Por mais de uma década, seringas, fraldas usadas e até tumores foram despejados dentro da Terra Indígena Taquaritiua, no Maranhão — sobre as nascentes de onde a aldeia Tabarelzinho bebia água. Em agosto de 2024, os Akroá Gamella decidiram que aquilo tinha ido longe demais: expulsaram à força o grileiro que ocupava a área havia quatro décadas e desligaram dois lixões municipais que funcionavam dentro de uma zona úmida protegida internacionalmente. As retomadas hoje restauram o território com práticas agroecológicas, reflorestamento de espécies nativas e recuperação de nascentes. Mas a violência continua.
Mulheres Krahô lideram guarda indígena para proteger território em Tocantins
Treze mulheres Krahô compõem o grupo de vigilância Mē Hoprê Catêjê para proteger os 303 mil hectares da Terra Indígena Kraolândia, no Tocantins, pressionada por madeireiros, caçadores, carvoarias e fazendas de soja e algodão. Durante quinze dias por mês, elas percorrem o território desarmadas, identificam sinais de invasão e encaminham as denúncias à Funai. A iniciativa nasceu da troca de experiências com outras guardiãs indígenas e segue protocolos baseados nos modos de vida Krahô. Além das ameaças externas, as integrantes enfrentam críticas dos homens de suas aldeias por deixarem temporariamente os cuidados domésticos para assumir funções de proteção territorial.
Kapinawás: meio século de luta pelo território sagrado no Vale do Catimbau
Até os anos 1970, ninguém no vale do Catimbau se dizia indígena — eram “caboclos”, sem nome nem terra reconhecida. Isso mudou em meio a uma guerra com grileiros, ocasião em que os moradores dessa área do agreste pernambucano encontraram uma escritura imperial na qual constava a doação daquelas terras aos seus antepassados indígenas. Cinquenta anos depois, surgiu a Terra Indígena Kapinawá, mas agora com um novo conflito: a criação do Parque Nacional do Catimbau, sobreposto ao território e limitando o acesso aos locais sagrados. Hoje, enquanto lutam para recuperar seus santuários, os Kapinawá desenvolvem um laboratório de recuperação da Caatinga, cultivando viveiros e plantando mudas por todo o território.
Jovens Yanomami recorrem a drones para vigiar seu território amazônico
Como vigiar, a pé e de canoa, um território do tamanho de Portugal? Foi essa pergunta que levou a Hutukara Associação Yanomami, em 2022, a apostar em algo inédito: ensinar jovens Yanomami e Ye’kwana a pilotar drones. A urgência decorria de uma invasão de 20 mil garimpeiros em 2019, durante o governo de Jair Bolsonaro, que desencadeou uma crise humanitária. Poucos anos depois, a combinação do monitoramento por drones com operações de desintrusão empreendidas pelo governo Lula reduziu em 91% as áreas de extração de ouro na Terra Indígena Yanomami.
Como mulheres Bakairi revolucionaram o combate aos incêndios no Cerrado
O som lembrava chuva chegando — só que era fogo. Foi assim que os Bakairi descreveram o incêndio de 2018 que devastou parte de seu território em Mato Grosso, enquanto aguardavam socorro. Da tragédia nasceu uma brigada voluntária hoje formada, em sua maioria, por mulheres — de adolescentes a avós —, treinada por um bombeiro aposentado. O resultado: quatro anos seguidos sem grandes incêndios na Terra Indígena Santana. A poucos quilômetros dali, outro povo sem essa mesma estrutura viveu o oposto — prova de que, no Cerrado, ter ou não uma brigada pode ser uma questão de sobrevivência.
Povo Pataxó restaura áreas degradadas para formar corredor ecológico no sul da Bahia
No litoral onde os portugueses avistaram o Brasil pela primeira vez, uma cooperativa Pataxó passou quatro anos replantando o pau-brasil e mais uma centena de espécies endêmicas da Mata Atlântica. Foram 210 hectares recuperados no sul da Bahia, em áreas da Terra Indígena Barra Velha do Monte Pascoal, metade deles com financiamento inédito do BNDES para sistemas agroflorestais — um raro caso de dinheiro público chegando a um projeto pequeno e indígena. Por trás desse avanço, porém, há uma luta: dos 50 mil hectares já demarcados para os Pataxó ali, apenas 9 mil estão, de fato, em suas mãos.
Guerreiras da Amazônia mostram que igualdade de gênero e conservação da floresta andam de mãos dadas
Na Terra Indígena Caru, no Maranhão, as Guerreiras da Floresta combinam patrulhas com mapas e drones com um trabalho de educação nas escolas e nos povoados vizinhos, buscando reduzir as invasões e a exploração ilegal de madeira. Formado em 2014 por mulheres Guajajara, o grupo complementa a atuação dos Guardiões da Floresta num território de 173 mil hectares que abriga também os Awá-Guajá e conserva um dos últimos trechos contínuos de floresta amazônica no estado. Os números comprovam seu esforço: o desmatamento na Terra Indígena Caru caiu de 2 mil para 63 hectares em apenas dois anos.
Projeto de gestão indígena pode ajudar a conservar a onça-pintada
Lançado em 2025, o projeto Ywy Ipuranguete prevê apoio à gestão de quinze terras indígenas, abrangendo cerca de 6 milhões de hectares em cinco biomas brasileiros. A iniciativa reúne monitoramento territorial, restauração e atividades produtivas, com potencial para beneficiar a onça-pintada ao proteger seus habitats e presas. Na Terra Indígena Caramuru-Paraguassu, na Bahia, lar do povo Pataxó Hã-Hã-Hãe, lideranças relatam que o maior felino das Américas voltou a aparecer após a retomada de antigas fazendas e a regeneração da vegetação.

title: Mexico cuts homicides by 51%, India hits gender parity in higher education, supermarket grows food on its roof
content:
Photo: Jakob Owens/Unsplash (CC0)
In today’s edition: Mexico has cut its daily homicide rate by 51% under the presidency of Claudia Sheinbaum, India has reached gender parity in higher education for the first time, and a Berlin supermarket is turning unused urban space into productive land.
Mexico is seeing a sustained decline in homicides, with July marking the lowest monthly average in more than a decade. Daily killings fell to 42.5, continuing a broader downward trend in violent crime, and the January-July average also dropped to its lowest level for that period since 2015.
Source: Mexico News Daily
The Health House by House programme is bringing basic care directly to communities, with 22.8 million home visits carried out between July 2025 and June 2026. More than 21,000 workers are checking vital signs, updating vaccinations and connecting people to specialist care, while the programme builds the health data infrastructure needed for a planned universal health service in 2027.
Source: Mexico Business
Women’s participation in India’s higher education system has grown faster than overall enrollment, helping the country reach gender parity for the first time. Additionally, over the past decade, expanding universities and colleges alongside stronger access for underserved groups has resulted in 31.5% increase in enrollment.
Source: DD India
JR Nagar in the south of India made rainwater harvesting pits mandatory for every building in 2010. Residents say the approach has kept groundwater levels stable and eliminated the need for water tankers, whilst advocates say the community offers a practical model for reducing water shortages and improving local water security.
Source: The Hindu
Hull 096, the world’s largest battery-electric ferry, has been delivered to its new home. Its 100% electric propulsion replaces diesel on the vessel, and points to a future in which battery power can be used at a much larger scale in passenger shipping.
Source: ABC News
New school food standards in England prohibit deep-fried items and set tighter rules for the food served to pupils. The changes aim to make healthier meals the default and improve children’s diets at school.
Source: BBC News
At 2,760 square metres, the Lankwitz REWE is now Germany’s largest rooftop farm. The farm makes use of hydroponic technologies: the lettuce varieties are grown with very little soil. The whole growing process takes a little over three weeks. Once cut, the greens go straight downstairs to be packaged and sold, both on site and in other stores in the city and region.
Source: The Guardian
Two UK solutions are using pictures to help people with disabilities communicate and understand information: Books Beyond Words uses wordless picture books to help people with learning disabilities share and discuss stories. TapSOS lets people who cannot easily speak on the phone contact emergency services through a smartphone app.
Source: BBC News
Farmers in Zimbabwe are using solar-powered lights, mobile cattle enclosures and beekeeping to keep lions away from livestock. The approach reduces attacks on cattle whilst giving communities practical ways to protect their livelihoods and coexist with wildlife.
Source: IPS News
Two years after four dams were removed, about 20,000 fall-run Chinook salmon have returned to the Klamath River in California and Oregon. The comeback points to the real-world impact of restoring river habitat, though drought, water use and remaining barriers still threaten long-term recovery.
Source: Inside Climate News

title: Connecting food systems at Portland Inaugural Indigenous food summit
content:
Lyric Aquino, Underscore Native News + Report for America and Nika Bartoo-Smith, Underscore Native News + ICT
For two full days earlier this month, community members from across Portland and beyond gathered to share knowledge and learn from one another during the inaugural Indigenous Food Summit.
Hosted by local Indigenous-led nonprofits, the summit came out of a labor of love and dedication to expanding access to first foods, land tending and food sovereignty.
“This gathering is not simply talking about the connected food systems, it’s practicing one,” said keynote speaker Nora Frank-Buckner, Nez Perce and Klamath. She helped organize the Native Grown and Gathered Food Expo in Seattle last year, which inspired organizers of this year’s Indigenous Food Summit.
“Our people have continued to carry the seeds, protect the knowledge, harvest the foods, and make place for one another,” she continued. “Our responsibility now is to make sure future generations inherit not only that knowledge, but also the land, the resources, the relationships, and power to act on it. Food sovereignty is how we remember who we are. It is how we take care of each other, and it is how we make sure future generations can set the table for themselves.”
As community members checked in at the Native American Student and Community Center at Portland State University on Sept. 9 and 10, they opened goodie bags that included a first foods cookbook compiled by the Native American Youth and Family Center, a hot sauce packet from Sakari Farms, a tea blend and smoked finishing salt. Over the course of the two days, just under 200 people attended.
Participants could choose from a wide range of workshops and sessions over the two-day summit, including cougar hide tanning, tea blending, wildfoods preparation, making natural cleaners, conversations about food in pregnancy and postpartum, and more.
Summit participants were invited to share meals that centered first foods and Indigenous chefs. Meals included wild rice and salmon or bison with a wojapi berry sauce, salmon chowder, elk stew and a three sisters salad.
On day two of the summit, a group of youth from the Siletz Valley Schools’ culinary program traveled to Portland and prepared four dishes to share before participating on a panel called “Nourishing Our Youth and Elders.” The four dishes included a cassava flour cracker with a honey huckleberry pudding; a butternut squash bisque with blackberry barbeque steelhead; a bison meatball with bluecorn polenta and huckleberry vinaigrette; and red heirloom popcorn tossed in duck fat with chili, lime and maple syrup.
“The hope for me doing stuff like this is just always that people know that they can participate in that reciprocity with our food systems and our medicines, and that they have every right to be in relationship with their prairies and their food forests and all of those wonderful beings that we get to coexist with,” said Emma Johnson, Cowlitz, Indigenous Traditional Ecological and Cultural Knowledge (ITECK) coordinator at Portland State University who helped organize the summit.
Johnson hopes that the summit becomes a regular occurrence, perhaps annual, along with supporting the potential for other similar summits across the region.
Tending to native and displaced plant relatives
For many, food sovereignty can feel hard to access in daily life, particularly for people living in urban areas, according to Johnson.
One of the goals with the Indigenous Food Summit was to make principles of food sovereignty feel more accessible to everyone.
“Everyone in this room carries something,” Frank-Buckner said during her keynote speech. “Some of you carry knowledge of plants or medicines. Some carry seeds. Some carry fishing knowledge, recipes or songs, language or stories. Some carry the responsibility of teaching our youth. Some know how to organize a market or a really awesome conference, write a policy, move resources, teach a class, build a business, or bring people together. Some are still discovering what has been placed in their hands. None of us carries the entire food system alone, and that is the point. Food sovereignty lives in the relationships among us.”
During the summit, participants were invited to take part in a series of hands-on workshops that centered around working with plant and animal relatives. While some congregated in the courtyard to learn about cougar hide tanning from Polima Joshevama, Hopi, and Amanda Freeman, Confederated Tribes of Grand Ronde, others gathered around tables of plants.
In one room, Adrienne Sampson, Navajo, founder of Waterlilly Botanicals, led participants in a tea-blending session. She provided a variety of herbs such as mullein, blue mallow flower, nettles and peppermint. Each participant walked away with a stress relief blend, a respiratory lung support blend and an immune boosting blend.
“Making your own herbal blends or using herbs is good for food sovereignty,” Sampson said. “It’s giving you that ability to take your wellness in your own hands.”
At a different session, participants passed around a basket of freshly harvested chanterelle and lobster mushrooms, while hearing from presenter Leslie Lekos, founder of Wildroot Botanicals, who discussed how to harvest food in nature. She also identified medicinal qualities of different fungi and plants. Mushrooms are high in amino acids, while goldenrod is high in antioxidants, she said.
Lekos shared recipes with participants as well, like a wild rice and chanterelle pasta and a goldenrod cornbread.
While much of the summit focused on cultivating, harvesting, collecting and processing first foods, other topics included weeds and invasive species.
There were conversations about tending to and working with non-native plants — called displaced or misplaced plants by some — in ways that honor the land and are careful to avoid disturbing native species. For example, simply ripping out non-native blackberries can sometimes harm other native plants that may be coexisting with them. Some presenters pointed to simply continuing to harvest blackberries as invasive plant management work.
As summit participants left with bags of tea blends and recipes and bellies full of first food-inspired meals, organizers hoped they also left with a sense of connection to other land tenders, medicine makers and community members dedicated to incorporating ITECK principles of food sovereignty into their daily lives.
“To see so many people embracing Indigenous foods and reaching back to those roots and embracing these different practices and these different activities, it’s really beautiful to me,” said Marie Knight, Confederated Tribes of Warm Springs. “Because as Indigenous people, this was how we lived our life prior to colonialism, and we’ve had to adapt over centuries of changes. And to see us coming back to this, adapted to this modern world, and bringing those ideas back, this is really beautiful to me.”
Decolonizing Your Diet
The rich scent of curry powder and jollof seasoning wafted through the air as retired professional chef Darius Mani Yaw prepared coconut milk collard greens with spring onions and fresh ginger, freshly ground corn polenta with garlic confit, spring onions, and African jollof powder and salt-bed roasted salmon seasoned with African nettle powder for a classroom full of eager students.
Darius Mani Yaw, a postgraduate Indigenous traditional ecological and cultural knowledge researcher, hosted a workshop at the Indigenous Food Summit about decolonizing the diet through ITECK and Indigenous internationalism frameworks.
“We’re able to learn so much about one another through food, through history [and] how our foods came to be,” Darius Mani Yaw said.
Darius Mani Yaw, who is Occaneechi, Black Saponi, Freedman and Giriama, told workshop attendees that he uses ingredients that span multiple cultures and encouraged his students to weave together traditional first foods from tribal nations throughout Turtle Island — and the world.
“So many cultures around the globe have three sisters,” he said. “So why is it that we can see the three sisters but we’re not able to see other first foods across these arbitrary borders?”
In his teachings, Darius Mani Yaw encouraged workshop participants to look into the framework of the American food system and spark change by starting or participating in community grassroots efforts.
“We are going to settler colonialists and begging for scraps and for pennies on the dollar,” Darius Mani Yaw said. “We need to start taking community action and better supporting one another and understanding.”
For Darius Mani Yaw, this starts by making the conscious choice to eat fewer processed foods and more traditional foods while also making sure his neighbors and community have access to similar tools.
“We have to start eating differently, caring for ourselves differently, growing our food if we can, or at least being in community to grow our own food, and supporting one another with these [traditional] knowledges and whatnot,” he said.
A common theme throughout the summit was community, which Darius Mani Yaw has tried to embody in his life and career. A retired chef of over 20 years, Darius Mani Yaw has made more than 10,000 meals for those in need and spent time in houseless encampments bringing meals and resources to his community.
“If I have a freezer filled of salmon, but my neighbor is not eating, what’s the point of having a freezer filled of salmon or bison or game or whatever that may be,” he said.
When Darius Mani Yaw reflected on the food summit, he highlighted the importance of sharing information between Native nations in what he calls Indigenous internationalism. For him, that includes combining his Afro-Indigenous ancestry. He said he hopes events like the summit will inspire others to discuss political action regarding food sovereignty, identity and cultural and traditional Indigenous knowledges.
“This was open to the community, and many of us were sharing our Indigenous knowledges across arbitrary borders. Whether we’re Native or non-Native, no matter our tribal affiliation, our European affiliate, it didn’t matter,” he said. “And here we are coming together specifically in this matter, having a meal, having an identity [discussion] and a political discussion over a meal, making medicines, tanning hides, and being able to show this together and be within community. And really, this was not only a sign of action and resistance, but it’s a resurgence specifically.”
This story is co-published by Underscore Native News and ICT, a news partnership that covers Indigenous communities in the Pacific Northwest.

title: From Used Flowers to Paper Pulp, This Mumbai Mandal Has Made Giant Ganpati Idols for 19 Years
content: For years, Sunil Mayekar has been troubled by what Ganeshotsav leaves behind in the ponds and lakes near his home in Vile Parle. He saw chalky sludge, flaking paint and idols that refused to dissolve for months on end. It is why, in 2008, his family's mandal decided to stop buying idols altogether. They started building their own giant Ganesha every year instead, out of the very things most people throw away. The year tissue paper replaced plaster of Paris The Bal Gopal Mitra Mandal is run by residents of Siddhivinayak Society in Vile Parle East. It has existed since 1989. Its approach to Ganeshotsav changed when sculptor Digambar Mayekar and his sons, Sunil and Rajesh, began experimenting with alternatives to plaster of Paris around 2008. Watching lakes turn murky after every immersion, the family decided their celebration should leave nothing behind. All three were trained in idol-making. They settled on tissue paper stretched over a bamboo frame, a method similar to the pulped-newspaper idols that households across India now shape at home on a smaller scale. Later, they began adding used flowers collected after the festival for texture and colour. Run by Siddhivinayak Society residents since 1989, the mandal went eco-friendly in 2008. How 30,000 tissue papers became a 22-foot Ganpati Building the idol takes months of unhurried, hands-on work. Bamboo sticks are lashed together with natural gum to form a towering skeleton. Layers of soaked tissue paper are then moulded by hand over this frame and left to dry in the sun. The process cannot begin until December, since the monsoon ruins the paper. In 2015, the family built a 22-foot idol from 30,000 tissue papers that weighed only 150 kg. Reports at the time noted that the paper-based idol dissolved far faster than conventional plaster of Paris idols, with the bamboo skeleton removed afterwards. Then came banana fibre, used flowers and new experiments The following year, Digambar and his sons scaled up further. They produced 11 such idols from a combined 3.55 lakh tissue papers. These were shipped to mandals in Goregaon, Andheri, Jogeshwari, Santacruz, Thane and Kalyan, priced between Rs 30,000 and Rs 70,000 depending on size. One was chosen that year as the neighbouring Mahimcha Raja. Marine biologists consulted at the time noted that idols made largely of paper pulp were comparatively safe because of the cellulose in them. The metallic paints still used on some idols remained a separate concern. Elsewhere, similar experiments have taken other forms. Some organisations now offer doorstep-delivered clay idols that are collected back for responsible immersion, while others make seed-embedded idols that grow into saplings after the festival ends. The Mayekars, though, have stayed close to paper and, more recently, banana fibre and flowers. In 2022, their 21-foot idol was built from banana fibre gathered from wedding halls since January, mixed with tissue paper so it would not crack, and mounted on a sculpted Garuda bird. This year's 25-foot Mumbaicha Peshwa idol was crafted from tissue paper and paper pulp recycled from last year's immersion. In 2026, last year’s Ganpati became part of this year’s This year, the Bal Gopal Mitra Mandal took the idea one step further. Its 25-foot Mumbaicha Peshwa was made using tissue paper and paper pulp recovered after the immersion of the previous year’s idol. The mandal now immerses its paper idol in an artificial tank, using only as much water as required to break it down. Once the immersion is complete, the paper pulp is collected and stored so it can be used again for the following year’s Ganpati. Over the past five years alone, its experiments have included banana fibre, alum, cocopeat, vegetables, tissue paper and flowers. What began in 2008 as an attempt to find an alternative to plaster of Paris has gradually become a cycle of reuse. For the Mayekars and their mandal, the celebration now includes thinking about what happens after visarjan, and what from one Ganpati can return in the next.
